Five Stars for Most Uses Update: The vendor and I connect through a post on his forum. Even though my 116 is long out of warranty he has offered to replace it. No one could ask for better customer service than that.

After hearing from the vendor I have reverted this to the five star rating that I wanted to give it originally, though with a caveat about the cables. The vendor says that the cables are for light duty, and that the device is intended for desktop use. I have to agree. Strapping it to the fork arm of a telescope mount while not rough service could be more than the designers intended. It is a fine product for the intended use. I like the driver support and the fact that there was no problem when I upgraded from Win 7 to Win 10. The XP install also works fine. I only am speaking about the drivers. I do not use the included software.

Below is part of the original review, describing the problem, the cause of the failure and a way to fix it. One of the two conductors from the yellow (video) jack broke inside of the plastic sheathing on the RCA plug. The expedient repair was to cut off the RCA plug and splice in a new one of a similar style. Then to add some bending resistance I cut a length of garden irrigation tubing, slit it length wise, tucked in the cable and wrapped the full length electrical tape. So far it works. The grabber is back in place and works normally.

Everything I said originaly including the option to look at less expensive alternatives, still goes. That said the EZCAP 116 is a good choice for the intended purpose and frees you crap shoot of finding drivers on the net.

Review-- The EZCAP 116 uses an eMPIA 2861 chipset, as good as any made, and the vendor has good email/forum support. When my original purchase developed an intermittent signal, they promptly sent me another one. The EZCAP 116 is at least the equal of the Dazzle that I once had and the support is much better. The 116 drivers work in Windows XP, Vista, Seven and 10. The image quality is as good as any I have seen.

Why then do I not give it 5 stars and why should you consider buying some other frame grabber. The answer is that the 116 and many other frame grabber-USB dongles use a very light wire gauge to connect the various jacks to the dongle and these wires can and do break. In this case creating first an intermittent signal loss and then total loss.

This dongle is strapped to one arm of a telescope mount and when the scope barrel is elevated or depressed the coax cable from the camera moves the video jack side to side a little. Over time this small movement was enough to break one of the conductors from the jack to the dongle.

Rather than buy another EZCAP116 my suggestion is to to look for a lower price dongle that uses the eMPIA chipset or perhaps an STK chipset. You may have to do a bit of searching to find out what chipset is in any product, though reviewers often post that information. Once connected to a PC, Device Manager will show in the device name or in the driver info the chipset.

The fragile cable is the only defect in the product however for me it is a critical defect. I willingly purchased it at a higher price than other dongles for claims of quality and support and the initial support was good.

In summary, the EZCAP.TV116, uses an eMPIA chipset, performs well in Windows XP through Windows 10. It is not rugged, the very light guage. It will not outperform dongles with the same chipset sold at lower cost by other vendors. Remember though that if you buy from EBay or Alibaba it is very much a buyer beware purchase, and of course slower delivery by China mail.as any I have seen. I was waiting for some distortion when it's put on blast but the blast was just dope vibes. The Feels and Portability

It doesn't feel like cheap plastic or the left overs plastics of a model airplane.

Waterproof

Singing in the rain? Yes with this you can.

Very nice, inexpensive water-resistant bluetooth speaker This is a very nice and compact speaker that has good water resistance and can easily be paired with a smart phone or other bluetooth device and used as an external speaker in the shower or outside, or really in just about any reasonable environment. It has a suction cup on the back which can be used to attach the speaker to a smooth surface.

The water resistance is stated to be IP65 here on the Amazon page, which is (in my opinion) very good. It can be deciphered as follows:

IP65 Explanation:
-- IP - International Protection, standard for marking to classify the degree of protection against intrusion
-- 6 - first digit indicates degree of protection against solid particles, on a scale of 1 to 6 with 6 being the greatest degree of protection, described as 'dust tight' and providing no ingress of dust and complete protection against contact.
-- 5 - second digit indicates liquid ingress protection, on a scale of 1 to 9. The 5 indicates protection against water jets, requiring that water projected by a nozzle (6.3 mm) against enclosure from any direction shall have no harmful effects, with a test duration of at least 3 minutes and specified water volume and pressure for the test.

Turning the speaker on or off is accomplished by holding down the power button and is confirmed by the speaker saying 'Power Off' or 'Power On'.

I used it in the shower although my particular shower has tile walls that do not allow for the suction cup to attach securely. Otherwise, it worked fine and was not affected by the moisture or water.

This little speaker has a very good audio quality. Of course, since it has only a single speaker, this is not a stereo speaker but the quality of the sound is very acceptable. Certainly it is considerably better than listening to something using the speakers build into most smart phones or tablets. The bluetooth profile used is A2DP (see wiki article 'List of Bluetooth profiles' for explanation, if curious).

It arrived at least partially charged but I plugged it into one of my USB chargers for long enough to make sure that it had a good full charge (a USB charging cord is included). It can be used while plugged in and charging (but should not be plugged into a charger when in a wet environment because it's necessary to open the rubber flap that otherwise seals the USB port from water intrusion). There is no indication provided as to when the battery is fully charged or what the remaining charge might be, which is a minor deficiency. I do like the fact that a rechargeable battery is part of the speaker and it will not require periodic battery replacement.

Instructions are included, written in mostly intelligible English (I enjoyed the statement, under 'Precaution', that \\"The Speaker has a fever phenomenon when normally operated or charging, it' s normal\\", which I assume means that the speaker may get warm at times when it's being used or charged.

When paired with my iPhone the volume of the speaker is mostly controlled by the phone (there is a more limited ability to raise or lower the volume using the controls on the speaker but the range of control is less than what you get from using the controls on your phone). The speaker also has controls to pause and start playback (if playing music files, for example), and for advancing to the next track or back to the previous track.

I will also point out that the volume ability of this speaker is moderate. It is not as loud (at full volume) as some bluetooth speakers, and the volume capability is not in my opinion sufficient to listen to this in the shower and overcome water noise adequately. It is just fine for placing on a desk or table next to where you are seated, and it will produce a comfortable volume level for normal listening. It is certainly not going to play loud enough for what many people may want for listening to music if you like to listen to music at reasonably high volume levels.

The speaker can also be used to answer phone calls when paired with a phone - an incoming call will automatically interrupt anything playing on the speaker, and the controls can be used to answer the call, or hang up when complete. The most recent phone number can also be redialed from the speaker.

The only display provided is a small blue LED located on the bottom of the speaker. It blinks continuously while paired and in use.

Mature sound in a sleek package I've owned the Envaya Mini for a couple of weeks now and I'm glad I pulled the trigger on this particular speaker. The sound is detailed, clear and the passive radiator adds a refined, subtle layer of bass. As far as small Bluetooth speakers go the soundstage is quite good.    PROS  - Sound quality  - Design  - Nice weight / build quality  - NFC & ability to connect multiple devices  - Pouch    CONS  - Battery life at maximum volume (which is lower than competitors)  - NFC not always works from first attempt  - Directional sound    As you can read from the above the Envaya Mini has a lot going for it, especially at it's price. Besides the sound, the design and feel are solid. When there's a nice tune on I catch myself staring at it sometimes ;). My notebook, tablet and smartphone are all connected to the speaker and I can easily switch from one to another when hitting pauze on the current source before pressing play on the next. Battery life is not as advertised and I get around 7-8 hours at normal listening volumes. At maximum volume it will last around 3 hours. The 3 color battery indicator is not linear and turns red when there is still lots of life in the battery. The angles at which you have the best sound quality are quite narrow compared to other designs. Maximum volume is not as loud as others and therefore I believe you should look at other options if you mainly plan to use your speaker outside. NFC is a nice function but from time to time I do have to tap my phone more than once before it works (Tested with Oneplus One).    COMPARISON  My roommate owns a Bose SoundLink Mini and I held some A/B listening sessions. The SoundLink has a warmer/darker sound whereas the Envaya sounds more neutral, crisp and clear. To my ears the the Envaya sounds more refined which is impressive considering the lower price tag.    CONCLUSION  Denon nailed the most important aspect of any speaker, the Envaya Mini sounds brilliant. Although there are drawbacks I think it is one ofthe better options around if you're looking for a Bluetooth speaker for inside use. I highly recommend that you have a look at the YouTube channel of \\"clavinetjunkie\\" who has a lot of comparison videos, including ones with the Envaya Mini. I decided to wait a couple of weeks before writing this review as some people are having units fail shortly after purchase. So far none of that here and I will update the review if it would become the case.    ***Update 04/25/2016*** Still going strong, no battery issues. Very happy with this purchase.

Not the worst but far from the best

Pro's

-the mic sounds great
-fit absolutely perfectly
-call button

Con's

-Sound really poor for music. Too much boomy bass, not nearly enough treble
-No mute button
-Not as good as many other headsets on the market

Quality and Comfort Monoprice Hi-Fi Over the ear review table of contents -

1. Intro
2. Packaging
3. Build quality
4. Comfort
5. Sound before and after burn in
6. 40+ hours of music / gaming
7. Pros / Cons
8. Conclusion

Intro -
Monoprice provided the Hi-Fi over the ear headphones free for review purposes.
When I received the headphones and after unboxing them I did a 2 hour comfort test in which I wear the headphones without listening to anything for 2 hours. After this I proceeded to listen to music for 4hours, followed with overnight burn in with pink noise, then another 4 hours of listening to music. The following week after receiving the headphones I wore them listening to music, movies, or playing video games for approximately 10 hours a day. During this review I will cover the packaging, build quality, comfort, and sound before and after the burn in, discuss my experience with over 50 hours of audio, pros and cons and last but not least my conclusion. So let’s get started.

Packaging
The outside of the box shows an actual size photo of the headphones. The art isn't too aggressive and highlights key features with emphasis on Hi-Fi. Opening the box you fix you find a plastic shell holding a hard case with the headphones inside of it. No paper work included. I was pleasantly surprised that the headphones were in their own hard case which has a good quality feel to it. Opening the zipper to reveal the headphones and cable.

Build Quality
The headphones are built really well and feel sturdy. The majority of this headphone is covered with soft touch rubberized plastic with chrome accents at the swivels. The ear pads are extremely nice and feel like they are constructed with memory foam. The ear pads can be easily removed to reveal the 40mm speakers. The build quality of the headphones has a slight plastic feel but they do not feel fragile or cheap.

Comfort
First thing I did when I received these headphones is put them on and wear them for up to 2 hours without listening to anything. I do this so that I'm not distracted by what I'm listening to and can determine the comfort of the headphones. I was able to wear these headphones for 2 hours without any discomfort. The following 5 days these were so comfortable I wore them for at least 10 hours a day for my music, movies, playing video games and making phone calls. I do have smaller than average ears and found the ear pads barely fit right around them however I had my wife test the fit and she said parts of the ear pads sit on her ear. Nonetheless these are very comfortable and everyone I had try the headphones on agreed they were incredibly comfortable. The one downside I had with the ear pads aside from being a little on the small side is possibly a personal problem; I tend to overheat easily therefore the leather ear pads would stick to my skin. As long as I stayed cool I didn't have any issues with the ear pads.

Sound before & after burn in
I listened to a wide range of music which includes RAP, Classical, POP and country for 4 hours before letting the headphones play pink noise at nearly full volume overnight. The first 4 hours listening the headphones had a wide sound stage with very clear bright almost shrill highs. The midrange is not muddy but the bass seemed to not have punch at times. After doing the overnight burn in, I listened to the same arrangement of music again for 4 hours. I noticed a small change with the highs, they weren't as shrill and the midrange seemed a little warmer though the bass was full it didn't however have a deep kick with some genres. The clarity and range of these headphones is remarkable. When listening to certain music you can hear clear separation of instruments, arrangements and in some instances they allowed me to hear audio that some of my other headphones didn't pick up. Overnight burn in with pink noise helped mellow these headphones out on the highs.

40+ hours of music and gaming
The sound isolation is remarkable with these headphone. I was able to test the sound isolation during my wife’s first 2 days of college the college had a DJ playing music loudly in the Cafeteria, putting these headphones on blocked out the majority of the music being played by the DJ. I listened to my music without any intrusion of the other music being played around me.
I wanted to make sure I got a good amount of time wearing these headphones for all types of listening activity to provide the best review I could. The music I listened varied from Les Miserables, Phantom of the Opera to 50 cent, Eminem all the way to Pop and Country. The listening experience was more than enjoyable as I found myself not missing my more expensive headphones I have available. Gaming with these headphones I played Battlefield 4, Brawlhalla, Guild Wars 2 and a few others. The headphones provided a great open sound stage which allowed me to accurately pin point audio within games and hunt down my opponents. Making a phone call with the headphones using the build in mic on the cable my voice came through clearly. The cable has plus minus pause and play buttons. The pause play button do as intended and if you double tap that button it also forwards to the next track. This was very nice when I didn't want to reach for the device.

Good fun versatile speaker which continues to impress. I have to say that this is one of my favorite things I have bought in a while. I looked at all the available bluetooth portable speakers (jawbone, Bose soundlink etc...) and all the "tailgate speakers" such as the ion Blockrocker and the Pyle line of portable speakers. As far as best bang for the buck, nothing comes close to this speaker.

I use it regularly at church whenever we have an activity without a built it PA system. Since it comes with both a wireless microphone and a wired microphone, it is very versatile. The wireless microphone has a slight buzz, but produces great clarity and sound reproduction. I'm not a musical performer, so for my purposes the slight hum is not an impact. The wired microphone was pretty flat and dull sounding, but when I hooked up a quality wired microphone I already owned, the tone was very good, comparable to the wireless. It's always amazing to me how well the sound projects, especially indoors. I have also been impressed with its effectiveness outdoors. I lead the fitness program in my Air Force squadron and was glad to have this speaker with me when the PA system we arranged for our Squadron fitness day never arrived. I was able to lead 250 Airmen in a 40 minute workout with the MCP-50 as my means of amplification, it was loud enough for everyone to hear my voice.

The music playback is my favorite aspect. I figured out how to load my CDG karaoke files onto my tablet, and then link my tablet via bluetooth to the speaker. It makes the perfect portable karaoke system for a day at the part, a camp-out, or anywhere you want to have fun. Everyone always asks me where on Earth I got such a cool speaker, their jaws drop when I tell them it came with all the equipment plus free shipping for $99. Go stroll through Bestbuy and look at their bluetooth speakers and see what $99 gets you there, it's not even close.

I was concerned when my wireless microphone stopped working on my after 4 months of ownership, I though "oh, here's the catch, it breaks easy and then you are stuck buying a new one." I contacted customer service and was delighted when they went out of their way to take care of me in a very personal and friendly manner.

This thing is so much fun, I find myself taking it with me to places where I have no reason needing it. You never know when you want to hang out and play some good music. It is so portable that you can really bring it anywhere without being too much of a burden. I've even hooked it up to a guitar and used it as a portable amp, though I recommend also using a battery powered effects pedal because the raw tone is a little low and can be kind of buzzy.

Overall, this speaker is the perfect solution to several needs that I didn't even know I had. I highly recommend you purchase it and see for yourself.

I ordered this thing because of the generally great reviews, prices, and simplicity of Wolverine. I was mostly interested in the negative scanner, but I decided to go ahead and shell the extra $30 for a photo scanner as well.

I decided to be objective about this, so I scanned the negatives and originals of 5 photos that were about 10 years old. The photo scan looks worse than when I snap an old pick on my phone for Facebook. In fact, the only advantage this scanner has over a phone snap is the straighter alignment of the image. Even that is tentative, as this device forces you to place the negative in a plastic strip with windows, and the slots on my negatives didn't quite line up.

Of course, the negative scanner produces better results--by lightyears--but the image quality is still just crap. My wife suggested that I shrink the image on my screen to its approximate print size, and that helped a little. But the image looks grainy and ancient at any resolution. The other thing that sucks about the negative scanner is that the tiniest dust particle or fiber takes up a quarter of the converted image. A brush is included for this sort of thing, but rebrushing all 10k or so of my family photos is literally impossible.

I remember feeling this way when flatbed scanners first became affordable. Then, as now, I had unreasonable expectations that the digital eye could capture a close approximation of my photos. I did some research this time and learned about DPI and megapixels. The industry standard for digital conversion seems to be 600 DPI, which is something like 3500x2500 resolution. This device was scanning my negatives at about twice that resolution, butit just doesn't make much difference. It's way better than the photo scan, but these devices do a TERRIBLE job of capturing the nature of the image.

I just don't understand why anyone would use this technology to convert their photos; and I don't understand how we're supposed to save our memories for the future, when this technology can't even come close to capturing the spirit of a printed photo.

If you're like me and want to cut your cable bill but still want to tune into some sort of television, this product will do it. First off, when deciding to buy an antenna visit antennaweb.org to view where the towers are at in your area, this will help you decide which range you need. In my case I bought the 50 mile amplified antenna. In my research, I found that amplified means that it is able to pull in more channels, at a further range, with better reception. My antenna in my area performs exactly as described, depending on many things I receive 15 - 20 channels.

When you are setting up your antenna, before you decide where you will mount it, test mount a few different spots using regular scotch tape to see where you get the best reception. I found that placing the antenna on a window that is facing the majority of the towers gave me the best results. For example, all my towers are north of my house, so mounting the antenna on the north side of my house worked the best. The supplied 3M tape works well and should hold up for a while. The attached coaxial cable should be long enough for most applications, but if you have to snake the wire all over your room you may need to purchase a double sided female coaxial adapter and extra coaxial cable.

I definitely recommend this product. But it can only perform as well as its environment allows. Many variables may affect the reception that you get at your location to include: distance from towers, interference from other sources, weather, and mounting location. Checking antennaweb.org will give you a good idea of the reception you can expect at your location.

After only three days, we got in touch with customer support. Though connecting the device to our wifi was not a problem, we quickly experienced connectivity problems. Essentially, we found it impossible to switch from one source to another, and the various applications kept freezing, whilst the music dropped out completely.

The only solution we found was to unplug and re-plug the unit in order to reconnect with a streaming source. Needless to say, this was a massive disappointment, and an even bigger frustration. When paying a premium price, one expects a premium product. B&O customer service were very quick to respond, and let us come to their store and pick up a replacement unit. This turned out to be the wrong model, so in the end, an employee from the B&O Retailer came to our house with yet another unit. The person made sure that the stereo was correctly set up, and working.

I guess we were hoping that our first unit was somehow faulty, as we loved the sound when it was working, and – of course – the design. Sadly, this has not been the case. On and off over time the unit kept freezing, and we had to unplug and re-plug to get connectivity back. Sometimes it even started playing German digital radio if you hit play by touching the unit. From what we could tell from the Beomusic app, the German feed came from the streaming app TuneIn to which we do not even have access. For those particularly curious, the channel in question was "Kulturradio rbb". After more than six months with frustration over not being able to just put on some music when we want, we contacted customer service yet again. Extremely Comfortable, Good Sound, Fair Build Quality. I'll break this review down briefly into three categories: Comfort, Sound, and Build Quality.

Comfort: 10/10. Bee's Knees. Cat's' Pajamas. These cans are the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn, and I've had my fair share of headphones. The ear pad is extremely comfortable and almost feels like there is nothing on your ear. It is like resting your pillow at the end of the day: pure comfort. The headband portion is very comfortable and doesn't become a nuisance when wearing the headphones for a while. Like I said before, these headphone are by far the most comfortable headphones I've had.

Sound: 9/10. The sound on these headphones is very full and crisp. You won't get crazy deep base on these, because that's not what they're built for, but the lows still fill out nice enough. The mids sounds perfect, the highs could be a little crisper but that's just something I tend to notice. If you're an audiophile then these probably aren't the headphones for you. But for the average consumer and even the avid listener, the sound quality is better than your average pair.

Build Quality: 8/10. The main components of the headphones are a hard plastic that holds up well to general wear and tear, and does a good job of not getting scratched easily. The headband has a soft mesh-type material on the underside that rests on your head. This material is very soft and acts as an nice cushion between your head and the headband. The earpieces are made from that signature plushy Bose foam material with a mesh oval pattern in the middle. The extending pieces on the inside look to be made from steel and show no signs of wear after a couple months of use. The headphones also fold up and twist into themselves so that they lie flat. With all those moving parts you would think that something is bound to break, but the folding mechanism seems very solid and doesn't show any resistance. My only complaint lies with the cable. The cable is detachable (good) andhas a nice mic and volume rocker on it (also good), but near the bottom at the male end I can't help but feel like the cable is very flimsy and prone to getting frayed even through general use. I haven't experienced this problem, but I've also been very careful in the ways I handle the ends of the cable. If I experience any problems with this I will be sure to update my review.

All in all, these headphones are a worthwhile investment for anyone who wants quality sound, comfort, and portability. I've never once regretted purchasing these and they've been great ever I bought them.

Quality antenna that should work well for you I live about 15 miles east of NYC/Empire State Building where most HD TV signals in my area are transmitted from. In one of our bedrooms we have a Winegard FL5000 indoor Flatwave antenna which has up to a 35 mile range. As far as local stations go the Winegard works very well for channels 2-1(CBS), 4-1(NBC), 5-1(FOX), and 9-1(Myn) but has trouble with 7-1(ABC), 11-1(CW), and 13-1(PBS).

I decided to try this Onh antenna because it has an amplifier and extended range hoping it would help pick up channels 7, 11, and 13. I had mixed results and found that the amplifier did not help very much if any for me. The amplifier did help receive channel 7-1(ABC) which the Winegard could not but like the Winegard it could not receive 11-1(WB) or 13-1(PBS) even with the amplifier. Other than helping with channel 7-1(ABC) I found that the Onh actually worked better without the amplifier. This may just be that I am in a range where the amplifier is not really needed and could over power an already good signal.

Doing a bit of research I found that channels 7, 11, and 13 are very difficult to receive with an indoor HD antenna in the NYC area because they are VHF stations. VHF signals have long wavelengths so they need bigger antenna elements in order to pick them up. In order to pick up those stations I would probably need a larger attic or roof-top antenna.

Overall this antenna works about as well as the Winegard but if you are considering purchasing an indoor HD antenna I would suggest first trying a quality non-amplified HD antenna first since they are usually cheaper and may actually work better for you. If you are further away (more than 25-35 miles) from stations you want to receive then maybe an amplified model may help you. I purchased this antenna at a discount in order to try it out and give my feedback.

The speakers were pretty much in the right position I received my first "pair" of SleepPhones (black felt, medium) yesterday and used them last night while falling asleep, so the review is for my initial impressions and not long-term durability.

It took me a minute to figure out the proper way to wear them -- I think the label goes up by the top of your forehead, facing in a way that someone looking at you would be able to read it -- this leaves the speaker wire hanging down your back. The speakers were pretty much in the right position, but I did have to nudge one of them a little to get it in front of my ear.

My first experience with them was listening to a guided visualization/meditation, binaural ASMR style (ASMR stimulates a relaxing sensory response in some people). Right away, I was very impressed with the speaker quality. I would say it is as-good as my $200 on-ear pair, but far and away more comfortable for sleeping. The headphones become one with the pillow and are almost "invisible" in that sense.

I say "almost" because the headband itself, while a perfect fit for me (average size women's head), was a tiny bit uncomfortable and warm, but it's a minor detail overall and I can't really think of a better way to get speakers to stay on my head (except to try the molded in-ear headphones, which I've yet to shell out for). I'll add that I have tried LOTS of different headphones and never really found any of them to be comfortable for more than 30 minutes or so. The SleepPhones were far more comfortable, sounded great, and did not bother my ears at all! Given how comfortable they are, I am curious to try a headband made from a lighter fabric for daytime use. For night-time, however, the soft plush felt is the way to go, IMO.

Moving on... the cable is braided and although thin is nice quality and doesn't get twisted up like some of the thicker cable styles. There cable is long enough to place your playing device (iPhone, etc.) on the bed-stand, but I would say it is just long enough for this purpose and you can't really move. While you can purchase aux cable extenders, an extra foot of length would be nice to have and I can't see how it would add much to their manufacturing costs. I think this point has been made by other reviewers.

When my meditation ended, I woke up enough to take these off, meaning I did not sleep through the night with them. Judging by my experience, I expect that they would be comfortable for many hours of sleeping/wear and the only problem would be tangling yourself in the cable when moving in your sleep. I have fallen asleep with regular headphones (my v-moda on-ear) and the extended pressure causes discomfort on the ears that can last for an hour or more. I think the SleepPhones would even be suitable for side sleeping since I turned by head to the side while wearing them, and the speaker is so low-profile that it just blended into the pillow.

Overall, I have to give 5 stars when comparing these to the general quality of what's out there. You can tell a lot of attention went into making these and the price is reasonable too. I hope they hold-up because most of my cheaper headphones lose sound in one speaker after a while. If they last a year or even six-months of heavy use, I will be very happy and will have considered this money well spent for enabling my relaxation time.

I LOVE IT and how I messed up There's lots to review on this radio because of its many features, so for people who don't like long reviews, the short story is that it's WAY better than I'd ever hoped, that I highly recommend it both for emergency and for everyday use, and that readers should at least scroll down to the part where I tell how I messed up the initial charge, just in case they are no more observant than I am. It does everything they say it will, and does it better than any radio I've had.

Other condensed points for readers who are pressed for time:
** Keep the box in a 2 gallon Ziploc bag--it may come in handy some day (see below)
** If you want to listen to the radio, I *think* the manual says the radio works better NOT plugged in to the AC adaptor (if you ordered one) because it will cause some interference. True, not too much but some. Usually it's just a little hum and I often play the radio plugged in, but I think you're supposed to unplug it when you turn it off so the battery doesn't overcharge.
** Check the date on critical reviews, and look for reviews elsewhere on the net. I did and decided the current radio would probably be good, and I'm happy.
** READ THE MANUAL. It's short and very good.
** Be SURE to plug in the internal battery correctly and securely before the initial 6 hour charge, if you get the optional AC adaptor. Otherwise, you'll get no charge. This is how I messed up!
** PROS: Shortwave, AM/FM, NOAA weather; solar, crank, 2 AA battery charge, OR an optional AC plug; reading AND flashlight; cell phone charger and one or 2 more that I haven't tried. Good reception, at least to my satisfaction certainly (but I'm not radio savvy), small size that fits nearly anywhere and picks up stations nearly anywhere; lightweight for carrying in case of evacuation; and overall just very pleasantly surprised by the great value for the price.
** CONS: None yet. I don't know how it will hold up over the long haul, especially since I use it every day, and I don't know what will happen if I need service, and I haven't tried the cell phone charger. But the Kaito is cheap enough that even if I break something and have to throw it out, I'll have paid no more than I did for the 2 NOAA "desktop" weather radios I already bought, not to mention quite a few other radios which only picked up, or CLAIMED to pick up, NOAA stations. And if I do break it, I will probably buy another and try to be more careful. I don't think the value can be beaten.

Now for the details...
I had looked at this radio for many months or longer but was always put off by some negative reviews. They said it was flimsy, wouldn't pull in stations, etc. I kept looking for reviews all over the web and didn't see these criticism, and wondered why. Finally I noticed the dates of those critical reviews. They were from around 2012, and I didn't see those complaints in more recent reviews. So I figured that maybe the company did have some problems with quality control in past years, which they overcame. So I decided to take a chance. After all, it was a great price, and I have spent way over that on weather radios that didn't last very long either, and had no features except NOAA stations. And those weather radios are hard to find the right place for, unlike the Kaito which fits anywhere and so far seems to get great reception anywhere.

When I opened the box, everybody said, "Oh how cute!" I wouldn't care if it was uglier than homemade sin if it performed--and it does, way beyond anything I could have expected. I'm seriously impressed. This will not be an emergency radio, but my everyday radio now.

It IS cute, or rather I would say, stylish and thoughtfully designed. You can see the photos yourself, and it looks really good. I will say, however, that while it gives the appearance of being a really tough field radio, I would doubt it's that tough. Some pieces look a little flimsy, but I'm thinking of the metal sliding piece that turns on the reading light and flashlight, so this doesn't apply to any high-usage pieces. Since I intend to set it on a shelf or carry it out in the yard maybe to solar charge sometimes, I feel it's sturdy enough for my purposes. I wouldn't throw it in the back of a jeep and go off road--unless I had a case for it. The crank that some reviewers complained about seems very good to me, having had several crank radios or flashlights before. I haven't tried the solar panel yet, but in the nuclear reactor that we call a climate here, I'm thinking it will work pretty well. In the past, I didn't have much luck with solar equipment some years ago when I lived in a climate more suitable for habitation, so you be the judge of your local sunshine. I know people here who grow beautiful vegetable gardens in what I'd call the shade, i.e. just a few hours of sun a day, so it's a really, really sunny place. I'm not in a position to really criticize the solar panel yet so look at other reviews to find out about that, preferably people who don't live in Africa or on the Equator or near me.

That is one improvement the company might make. I think they are justifiably proud of this radio. Probably some talented people have worked hard on it. I really like to see a company take pride in their product, and try to respond to constructive criticisms to improve it, or even just to CARE if the consumer is satisfied. They seem anxious to make this product the best they can and solicit user feedback. If this little radio becomes a good seller as it ought, they might consider making a padded case, hard outside and padded inside, to sell as an accessory, with extra room for an AC charger, earbuds, whatever, and maybe a long shoulder strap. A good case like this would cost a good bit, but since this is, among other things, an emergency radio, some people might appreciate the convenience of a traveling case, instead of having to make theirown--because anything as vital as a radio in an emergency needs to be well protected from hard knocks and bad weather. For now, I'll just keep the box it came in to pack it in if I ever have to be evacuated or something horrible like that. The box would do fine actually instead of a special case if you only need to transport it on rare occasions, since the box protected the radio just fine during shipment, but I'd put it in a plastic bag to weatherproof it for such transport which could involve bad weather, chemicals, radiation, whatever. I put my box in a 2 gallon Ziploc bag and there's room left for cords or small electronics--plus the manual! So actually, selling an optional carrying case might not really be necessary, if you just keep the box for carrying.

HOW I MESSED UP

Before I forget, I should mention how I messed up, to spare others of my ilk (somewhat clumsy and careless--I can't be the only one) from this boo boo. The manual said to charge it for 6 hours using the AC adaptor (if you ordered one extra) before first use, so I did. There's an internal battery that must be connected before charging, and I did that, per manual instructions. I noticed that the battery access cover was just slightly akilter and I wondered why, but I plugged it in and waited impatiently for 6 hours. When I tried it out, not one thing happened! From having similar radios in the past, I thought batteries (3 AA batteries) would probably still work, so I opened the battery bay and saw that the internal battery, which I had plugged in, had become unplugged before I even started the 6 hour charge! I plugged it in more carefully to be sure it was well seated and tried again.

But after waiting 6 hours, I HAD to see if it would pick up any stations at all, so, well, I didn't wait for the proper 6 hour charge before I tried it, as the manual said to do. I figured I could always buy another internal battery if I mess this one up. I don't live in a great spot, far from everything, so I didn't expect much, and boy, was I amazed. It had the clearest reception of any radio I have, even the car radio (at least the stations I like--can't speak for the others). It picks up FM stations I never knew existed and in the evening scads of stations on SW1 and SW1. Shortwave stations are more limited during the day, which I think is to be expected, but the ones that do come in are loud and clear. My knowledge of shortwave is limited to using my father's set years ago and I expected to be constantly retuning the stations as they drifted in and out. To some extent, I do have to with the Kaito, but nothing like I did years ago. Besides, I consider this the full, interactive shortwave experience! So no, it's not digital, but I don't care. Also, this good reception is without the optional antenna, which I didn't order initially. I'm curious now to see if I could get even better reception with that.

I also like the small size of this jewel. It's easy to find a spot for it, and in this one radio I can switch from AM to FM to SW bands to NOAA weather (just to get the daily forecast fast), use emergency lights, etc., so it's terribly handy and works well for my limited space. I have two other AM/FM radios which I have to put in bizarre locations to pick up a few stations and I am getting rid of those. I have a couple of weather radios that I may give away or store since I don't have much space. This Kaito runs rings around all the others that I have, plus has shortwave and more charging options, a reading light, a flashlight, a cell phone charger (though the manual says don't expect too much of that, like using it with a totally dead battery, yet they say it works within limitations), and can use the optional external antenna, plus another couple of features I haven't looked at yet.

I also have an Eton American Red Cross radio but I was never really happy that it had no shortwave. I really wanted shortwave because I justlike listening to the weird stations, but also because if there were a big disaster in my area, I still might be able to pick up SOME news from other countries or locations. The Eton doesn't seem to have AM/FM either, now that I look at it. It quit working so I put it up and later realized what might be the problem, right before I was ready to throw it out. I just now cranked it and it works find by that method, but only for weather, so I wouldn't recommend it, unless NOAA weather is all you care about. If so, an Eton would be fine, but why not get something you can use every day?

Incidentally, desktop weather radios that are so popular can also be fragile. I now have a Midland which I got to replace my first "desktop" NOAA radio that was promoted by the local TV station. I can't remember if that was a Midland too or not, but I knocked it off the table and ruined it. A teeny plastic piece held the antenna connection and that broke, so I had to toss it.

The Kaito's weather radio picks up several stations in my area, and I just had to turn the knob from stations 1 to 7 to find the one I prefer, no codes needed and none of the ordeal of going through every state and county in the USA to find my station, as I have to do with my Midland weather radio. Again, NOAA comes in extremely well. I forgot I have yet more crank weather radios which don't pick up anything at all. I guess that's 2 more radios I can toss now. Pros:
+Audio Quality - For bluetooth headphones they offer very good acoustics, matching mid level Sennheiser (~$50).
+Noise Cancellation - Using the different sized ear tips, when they fill the entire ear canal they offer very good passive and active noise cancellation.
+Price - These headphones are cheaper now than when I bought them and for ~$20 they aren't terrible if you use them gently.
+Customer Service - When I contacted customer service when my pair broke, they responded quickly and courteously.

Cons:
-Quality - The pair that I had broke within 11 months and the replacements that they sent me broke within a month. I can understand having 1 pair break over time due to wear and tear, but the replacement breaking within a month is some QC issues.
-Cable Length - For some people who want long cables they might see this as a plus, but if you're trying to use this when working out the cable length is too long and gets caught. While wearing these the cable would rest on the top of my spinal column (top of the back, bottom of the neck).
-The placement of the controls - Due to the controls being positioned more on the right, the cable will sway to the right due to the weight which over time gets to be annoying when running or doing anything active.
-Fit - This is a very big one when looking for headphones for active workouts. The fit of these headphones are a very big hit or miss, unless they're placed very well you will have some movement. They come with small clips that go behind the ears which help alleviate this problem, but they're incredibly flimsy and will most likely break even with gentle handling. Once these clips break then you're left hoping the fins that brace the headphones will be good enough to keep them in place. More than likely for less rigorous activities they will (weight lifting, stationary bike, etc.) however if you're trying to run with these things they most likely won't stay in.

Overall if you're able to live with the cons and want a cheap pair of blue tooth headphones these aren't bad, but for a few dollars more you can get yourself a better pair of headphones for the gym.

Great Bang For the Buck I bought this speaker at Costco on a whim because it was on sale. Im so glad I did.  This stereo BT speaker rocks!  This speaker provides an amazing bang for the buck. The sound quality is insane for a portable, waterproof speaker. It's ridiculously shockproof too. The sound is very clear, rich and full, but if I had one minor criticism, I'd say it was a bit darkly colored; although there is adequate low-end, the highs could be a little brighter. That's easily handled with a tweak of an equalizer though. Again, that's just imo, ymmv, depending on your individual preference; I just happen to like hearing crisp cymbals, for example.  BTW, I've seen people, and even professional reviewers, state that there's a passive radiator on the back; it's not. It's an active subwoofer. That's probably why it outputs a whopping 24 watts - those low freqs take some oompf to crank out.  That said, i cant see anyone being disappointed in the sound, especially if someone in your camping trip brings a $250 Bose BT speaker to the party. This happened: Most people there agreed the the quality of the two was about the same. Some liked the Ecostone, about equal number preferred the Bose (I personally liked the highs coming out of the Bose a bit more). But here's the kicker: if your Ecostone gets left out in the rain overnight, or dropped off a table or tailgate, you aren't worried. The Bose owner just added a couple of pounds to the local landfill.  ThE Ecostone plays loud enough to fill the largest of campsites or backyards without distorting. Now all this sound quality is especially good, because you do sacrifice some portablity for all this power and sound clarity. It's 3.5 pounds, btw, so it's not terribly convenient to strap to your backpack on a hike.  Added nice touches: The built-in flashlight is nice. The button for it appears at first to be in a weird spot, until you carry the speaker by its handle. If walking in the dark, your thumb is right over the button, so you can turn thelight on without having to see it. But its not nearly as bright as say, a Cree torch. Also the ability to charge a cell phone is handy in a pinch.  Overall, I'd give this 4 stars if the price was considerably higher. But adding the Value Factor into the mix, it's hands down a 5 star product.

1x Velcro Carrying Strap

You can most certainly tell SHARKK took pride and no shortcuts with its packaging and included accessories. There's definitely pride here in the way they present this speaker to it's customers. I've purchased Bluetooth speakers that did not include the adapter and ask you to use your smartphone adapter. Nice touch by SHARKK! The Velour carrying bag and Velcro strap are excellent additions and really give the entire package an upgraded feel and look. Everything you need is included and then some. I posted a few pictures.

Now to the meat and potatoes of this powerful waterproof speaker.

If you need a speaker that is rugged, dust and waterproof, plays music beautifully and has useful features, then you can not go wrong with the SHARKK 2o. It's covered with a nice hemp/cotton material that I've read is also made of recycled plastic bottles. It has a Real bamboo wood strip across the back with the company's branding (Marley). The front grill is metal with the company logo on the bottom right. The logo lights up blue when the unit is on. Flashes blue when in pairing mode & flashes between red & blue when battery is low. The controls are EASY to use & understand even for a first time user of Bluetooth speakers. The Bluetooth button also acts as a call button & pause button for music as well as pairing although I'm not sure why it's called the bluetooth pairing button due to the fact the speaker goes into pairing mode as soon as you turn it on.

The micro USB port for charging is under a silicone flap on the right back/side & an Aux 3.5mm input is on the left side, also under a silicone flap. It has 2 silcone "feet" on the bottom so the unit isn't directly on the surface its placed on & they absorb much of the vibration from the bass of the music which could be an issue if there are other items on the table such as coins etc...that would rattle around if they weren't there.

I believe this speaker comes in 2 versions. I have read that this speaker is also available with 4, 1" drivers however which is either an earlier version of this device or what is being bought overseas, I'm not sure. In closing; if you have the money to purchase a "higher end" Bluetooth speaker, give this one serious consideration. In my opinion this is a very good buy for its purpose, for playing music. I Was Afraid Of This Happening Mr. Noontec goes and asks me for a review, probably just to boost the sales on another set of his 'phones, and that's not why I do this. I'm loyal to to the audio community, and then what does he go and send me,........

I've been so determined to thoroughly test this product that I've brought it to two other recording facilities owned by associates of mine, and I pushed them on a few other seasoned engineers, listening through their equipment just so that I could gather more opinions on them. I had to create an adapter from a Tip-Ring-Ring-Sleeve 3.5mm jack, to a 1/4 inch stereo plug in order to test this way, but it allowed me to plug into a better signal than a phone or MP3 player for testing purposes.

What you'll be buying is just another good looking set of in ear 'phones, they appear to be what you should expect in this price range. You'll see the flat cable because that stands out right away. I'm not going to push flat or round on you, you decide, but this cable is not going to tangle as much and it's as close to perfectly quiet as they come. For you tall guys, this is a longer style cable and they've also included a removable clip on it. You'll also receive a hard shell case for them.

What's going into your ears is a small, lightweight earpiece. I think that this is important, because all of the 'phones that fall out of my ears, are the heavier models. These stay in my ears much better than most BlueTooth sports models do, and I think it's simply because of gravity, those are heavier due to batteries and circuitry. These are 100% perfectly comfortable in my own ears.

I haven't had a lot of phone conversations while wearing these, but my testing proved them to be adequate for it. I'm a bit of a dinosaur and feel like I'm tech support or something while talking on a headset.

So what Mr. Noontec sends me, is a set of good, high quality in ear 'phones that my associates and I agree sound extremely accurate at reproducing audio for their price. These are one of the best sounding in ear 'phones that I've ever heard. But I'm not talking about what is “liked”, you're free to like whatever you want, I said accurate.

What I'm talking about is when monitoring a drummer, miked up in the drum room through a console for instance. No EQ, just a good drum kit, with 14 microphones on it and ready to be recorded, with this headset connected to the headphone amp from the console along with the typical studio headsets to make comparisons. These sound like you're in the room with the drummer, I checked them extensively and they brought a smile to the faces in the two other facilities also, thumbs up, and at this price, two thumbs up.

Perspective, what this means to most users is that from any device that you plug these into you will be hearing very close to the true sound from it. If the recording or your device is poor quality, you'll hear that, and the converse is true also. I think that this is always a good thing, but opinions vary. Just remember that facts and opinions are not the same thing.

I can't rate the long term durability as I've only had these about ten days now, but nothing about the quality of this headset worries me either. I ran them up to painful listening levels and also let them run overnight twice.

If you want to hear what the actual recording sounds like from your in ear headphones, I recommend these. If you want to hear that and then tailor the sound to what you yourself like to listen to, I can recommend these. I don't recommend these for animals outside of the human species though, I cannot universally endorse this product after all and this is what I was afraid would happen. I don't stamp 5 stars onto products and yet, what Mr. Noontec has sent me, leaves me no choice.

I do believe that about 97% of the population will be happy with these 'phones and will agree that you don't need to spend any more than this on a set of in ear headphones. The other 3% of the population likely have some malady and are just unhappy about everything. If you don't like the music that you hear from this headset you should blame us, because you don't like how we did it in the studio.

Great BT Receiver for price I will start by saying that this Bluetooth receiver works well and is very compact. There are some specific details that I was concerned about for my application and I will clarify some of the functionality of the device.

The audio quality from the device is surprisingly decent (the paired device is in very close proximity during operation). There is an album that was particularly affected by lossy audio codecs even when ripped from Vinyl in 320Kbps MP3, and when playing a lossless format from my paired phone, there wasn't much of a perceivable difference in quality versus plugging directly into the headphone jack on the phone at the same volume.

The blue light behind the multi-function (Play/Pause) button is not particularly bright meaning that it doesn't consume much energy during operation. That also means that when I am attempting to turn it on/off in direct sunlight in my car, I am connecting via trial and error and I cant tell what stage the device is in by just looking at it.

The battery lasts a sufficiently long amount of time.

The +/- arrows on the edge of the device are handy. This is one of the features I was looking for most in a BT receiver device, and it was not expressly detailed in the description of this device. The buttons act as forward/back for tracks with short presses. They then act as volume up/down with long presses. This works well for me because when I am using my phone in my vehicle for longer trips, it is being used with a GPS app that is up on the screen constantly and to change tracks, I must use the interface on the phone. This device allows me to change tracks without even looking at the screen because I can feel for the device and then change the track with the physical buttons.

The device will wait in a standby mode for a few minutes if turned on and not connected to any paired device or if the paired device is disconnected. It will automatically attempt to connect to the paireddevice when powered on. The battery level of the receiver is relayed to the paired device if the paired device supports it.

The mic on the device itself works well enough but I have not tried it with excessive exhaust/road noise.

A cheap addition that would add value in my opinion would be a simple mounting solution other than the double sided headphone jack like a square of double-sided foam tape or velcro pad to allow mounting on to a certain part of the dash.

The reason for 4 stars instead of 5 is solely based in that I can't quickly turn it on when I get into my car, the button has to be held for 5 seconds. Even if I could wire it to turn on when it receives USB power and then wire a USB charger to be activated with my ignition when I start the car so that I do not need to hold the button to use it, that would be great as well.

Walkman has walked a long way! The last and only Walkman I owned was back in the mid-80s. That was a cassette tape player with headphones. Things have surely come a long way!

I was drawn to this because of its hi-res quality. So far I've not been disappointed on that score. The sound is excellent, probably better than my other equipment can reflect. The unit is light but not flimsy--extremely portable. While a touch screen would have been nice, things are easily navigable, much after the fashion of a digital camera. I'm a Mac user, and while some Mackies have complained that they can't export to this device from iTunes, I don't find that to be a hindrance. Unlike the iPod, the Walkman shows up on your desktop as an external disk. You can double click on the Music folder on the device, and simply drag files from your iTunes music folder without the mediation of iTunes itself. The Walkman's software makes good sense and organization out of the iTunes folders. In short, you can bypass iTunes altogether. While some may not like this, I find it gives me better control in loading just what I want onto the device. Using the Walkman disk this way, you can even rename folders and files on your Walkman when it is connected to your computer. I'm not even going to bother with the special Mac software for loading music files.

What else? No issues with Bluetooth connection. High-quality sound. Ample storage for such a portable device--although I'll be glad when I can fit my whole AIFF music library on a tiny player. Much as I've enjoyed my iPods in the past, I think this is better for those interested in one thing: listening to their music in high-quality format.

I can't hear what you're saying over this Active Noise Cancellation I want to start this review by saying that Monoprice sent me these headphones free of charge for review.
With that in mind the price point for these headphones is spot on. If one was looking for a set of headphones that were as functional as they were aesthetically pleasing, these would be the ones to look for, especially for $99.

The box these headphones come in is very clean, minimal and well built. The important information is written on the back of the box with listings such as 32 ohm impedance in passive mode, 100 ohms in Active Noise Cancelling and Bass modes. With up to 15dB of active noise cancellation on a 20Hz-20KHz frequency response these headphones are great for those long flights with screaming kids and noisy neighbors.

These come with a very nice semi-hard carrying case for ease of travel. Inside are the headphones with a nice 1.4m(4.5ft) cable with inline microphone and controls. In my particular case there were 2 AAA batteries, necessary for the active noise cancellation and bass modes. You can listen to music, videos, etc without the need of the batteries, passive only mode, but you will mist on the 15dB noise cancellation. These do a great job of eliminating outside noise on their own being close-backed headphones but that ANC mode is all the more better with 4 mics working to cancel outside noise.

Some cons are they are a little tight on the head, even though they are around the ear style headphones. The volume control does not work on Android, but the play/pause does. If not using the included case, which is a little bulky, the headphones do fold up for easy travel inside a smaller bag. Although the headband and ear cups are leather padded, they are a little uncomfortable after extended use.

All in all I really like these headphones, they are not as good as my Big Brand Name headphones, which were half the price but that’s a different matter entirely. If I was in the market for a great pair of close-backed, Active Noise Cancelling headphones for a decent price, these are the ones that I would look for and eventually purchase. The pros outweigh the cons with this pair and I would gladly recommend them to anyone else looking for a decent pair of noise cancelling headphones.

Unrivaled style and sonic performance for this price. The Momentum 2.0 is absolutely the best portable headphone I've ever listened to. Period. Sennheiser has managed to accomplish a rare feat by producing a seat of headphones that are both aesthetically appealing as well as sonically impressive all for under $400.  I upgraded from my Shure SE-215's after finding that I wanted something that could deliver more in terms of soundstage. I tried the Bowers and Wilkins P7, Master and Dynamic MH40, and V-Moda Crossfade 100. Then came the Momentum 2.0.  The sound signature on these is downright impressive for a closed back headphone. The bass is punchy and tight (albeit marginally loose in the sub-bass area) and carries some serious heft in songs like Massive Attack's "Angel".  The mid range is equally impressive and isn't overpowered or muddied by the bass response - they are remarkably clear. Snare drums are crisp and snappy, pianos are seductively warm, and picked guitars are a joy. Fleetwood Mac's "Dreams" produced a serious "Wow!" Moment for me in this department.  The highs are a bit rolled off at the very top, but I can't complain too much, as I don't find it taking much away from the headphones. They still have plenty of sparkle to them. I still hear a decent amount of decay in cymbal strikes and plenty of detail, which allows these headphones to be light and airy when needed. This is extremely apparent in Tycho's track "Awake". In my opinion, the roll off on he high end prevents these cans from being too sibilant and fatiguing and lends a bit of a warmer sound. Not a bad thing - but it will bother those who want a less "fun" headphone and desire something more clinically accurate.  Oh, and these headphones look great. I bought the ivory ones because I just couldn't resist the white contrasted with the brown leather headband. Style is subjective so I won't go further here.  As far as comfort goes, Sennheiser deserves a serious pat on the back. I found the P7 and Crossfade to beway too clampy and had to take them off, as they were giving me a headache after 45 minutes or so. The MH40's, although built impressively well and absolutely gorgeous, were simply WAY too heavy. No go. The Momentums are incredibly light and not at all too tight. I have worn them while studying for multiple hours at a time and not once have I found them uncomfortable or too hot. It's easy to forget they're on your head.  Bottom line: these headphones sound wonderful. They are not the most accurate headphones on the market, but Sennheiser has found a very pleasing balance between clinical accuracy and a lush, welcoming sound that is difficult to accomplish without sacrificing much of anything in regards to clarity and performance. And they're gorgeous and comfortable, to boot.

Worth Their Asking Price I work with headphones all the time and I particularly like active noise canceling (ANC) phones. The gold standard is Bose but you pay a premium if you want those phones. One of the issues I have seen with headphones is that many manufacturers claim to have noise canceling phones when they really are just noise isolating phones. These phones by AGPtEK are true ANC phones and while they are a far cry from Bose they are actually good headphones.

These are very lightweight and reasonably comfortable phones. The padding on the ears is a little stiff but they are not hard. I can wear them for a while and they do not get too warm and they do not pinch my ears. These are over-the-ear phones and they fit properly. I do not like the headband, though - there is no padding on the headband and if you have thin hair (or no hair) on the top of your head these have no cushion at all and they feel like they’re scraping when you put them on though they are fine once fitted.

I have noticed that these phones are not the very best when it comes to the sound profile, but they are certainly acceptable. The best way to describe the sound is “subdued”, though these phones are really strange in how they present sound. There are tracks I have loaded up and listened to that sound slightly muffled and quiet and at the same time I can hear details I never before noticed with any other headphones. I am not sure what to make of the sound profile as these sound different than any other headset I have used but they still sound good. An audiophile will not like these phones very much, but most will find these to be acceptable. I think the sound profile could use a boost in the midrange?

These headphones have the electronics in them to actively cancel low-frequency noise. So, when you have these on and you are on an plane or you are in a noisy car, turning on the ANC function drastically cuts down on engine and road noise so that you can hear the music better or you can enjoy a quieter ride. I have a fan I use to generate white noise, and I tried these phones’ ANC function with the fan on. The ANC circuit did cut a good portion of the noise, though nowhere near as much as my Bose set does. That said, these do a good-enough job of cutting sound to make them effective.

I like the fact that the phones continue to work even when there are no batteries. The only thing the batteries affect is the ANC function.

This headset does one thing correctly that many other phones I have tried has gotten wrong. So, the ANC function means a substantial volume boost to music, and the claim is that the overall volume level remains the same. That might be true but it is deceptive. This headset does it right - the volume of the music is boost just enough to sound exactly the same whether the ANC is on or off.

The most important function with this set is the ANC and it does work, and it works better than some other sets I have seen and used.

I use a lot of ANC phones and this set is probably the best value of those I have seen and used. It is not perfect but the flaws are small when you consider that these cost so little. An outstanding amplifier realistically priced with high end ambitions. I live in the UK where this amplifier comes from . I have been using the Caspian Series M2 Integrated amplifier, initially as a stop gap measure until I could afford to have my high end system overhauled . That was three years ago. I am still using it with the Caspian cd player used in a balanced mode and a pair of Triangle Signature Delta speakers and I feel no urgent need whatsoever to have my Naim amps and Mark Levinson cd player overhauled. Why ? May you ask . Simply because the sound I am getting is as good as my so called high end super expensive system!
The Roksan amp is so good that it will make you think it's an amp costing several thousands $ more. The soundstage it produces is as good as my Naim 250s and 135s. It will drive difficult loads without any problem but more importantly, it can be happily partnered with a wide range of speakers. The funny thing is that the cables I am using cost more than the amp and cd player combined! You would think that the Kimber bifocal XL speaker cables would show up the Caspian M2 shortcomings. Well, they don't. As a matter of fact, the combination seems to be a perfect match with the internal Kimber wiring of the French speakers being used as well. The conservative 85 watts power per channel quoted by the maufacturer do not necessarily reflect on the loudness level this amp can subjectively produce. You can have Lady Gaga full blast at high levels if you wish and if you are prepared for a lawsuit with your neighbours. Your speakers might go first, and your wife next but not the amp which I believe has a very sophisticated protection circuit, unllike the Naims of earlier years.
What makes this amp so special is its versatility and ability to reproduce any music regardless of the genre. Whether you listen to Grace Jones, Count Basie or WA Mozart, it will invariably communicate the message and emotions contained in the music. The preamp section is so good that you can play older recordings without having to worryabout the potentially obstrusive background noise. Alfred Cortot playing Schumann Carnaval recorded in 1928 sounds amazingly fresh and exciting and Maria Callas singing Abigail in that impossible Verdi aria from Nabucco is simply out of this world. Mind you, using the Kimber Kable all round helps as well.
I hope that by now I have convinced you about makes this British amplifier so special. By the way, it is the top recommended amplifier in the UK What Hi Fi magazine for amps costing £ 1500 and above. So, even if you buy it in the US, it will not cost you that much more at $ 3000 a piece. It retails for £ 2000 in the UK.
I think anyone looking for a top performer at an affordable price should put this amplifier on their list for auditioning. I wonder if any dealer would dare use it with a pair of Wilson Audio speakers ! That would be an interesting alternative to the overpriced Naim Statement !
So, to sum up my review, the Caspian M2 series 2 amplifier is probably the best kept secret in the hifi world .
PS: I am not a member of the British Audio Indusrty trying to promote British equipment ! I am simply an ordinary guy who takes a genuine interest in high quality hifi products at a realistic price.

I will leave part of the previous review in case anyone else experiences static and/or pops  The D1 is sturdy, relatively light, and makes a notable difference when used in place of even the best on board DACs, at least on Windows and Linuux machines. I use it primarily for editing interviews and listening to music and it serves admirably for both. I have used it with Beyerdynamic 990 pro 250 headphones, Audiotechnica ATH M30s, and powered monitor and the sound quality is excellent through all. Interviews and talking heads are clear, no background noise at all (aside from noise introduced by clients who assume HVAC noise will just magically not be heard behind their mumbling). I listen to an eclectic mix of music; all genres sound good, with a cappella, classic, jazz and acoustic pop/rock offering new layers I had not previously experienced. Metal and rap do not have the over amplified, distorted bass that purchasers of Beats seem to like, but I suppose you could hook Beats up to it and still enjoy the perfectly delivered signal, much like a dog would eat chateaubriand but is content to lick it's own ass.   ORIGINAL (edited): I do not usually write reviews for products that seem to be faulty.  The product seems sturdy, the construction is fine, it is aesthetically non-offensive, has the inputs and outputs I need/want and might be a good DAC/Amp, if it worked properly. The amp is too weak to effectively power Beyerdynamic 990 pro-250s, or rather, the cans are about a quarter of the volume of speakers run through the same amp. And the D1 I received, as other reviews have noted, would randomly generate bursts of static. So possibly a lemon, I thought, although with devices hooked up to a computer there are other possibilities. So I explored all the possibilities in hardware and software, swapped the D1 into a stereo system, tried it on other computers, redid all the software setting for bit rate and depth. The static is not just an inconvenience, though it is one when editing video/audio file: I am fairly sure the static blew out a pair of Mackie monitors.  As I am not sure what other reviewers were running as a source, I will note I was running the D1 on a Windows 8 then a Windows 10 system. Both OSes demonstrated the static. Best HDMI Cable on the market!! The QUALITY of the HDMI cable you use in your setup matters. To verify the quality of a HDMI cable, one test that is performed is called the "eye" test. I bought the Fusion4K cable because they proved their quality by showing their eye test results.
Doing a fair amount of research on this topic I learned the following:
As the length of the cable increases, the signal interference also increases. Think of this like the "resistance" of the signal in the cable increases the farther it has to go. Also, the more data you pass through the cable (bandwidth) the more interference you'll see as distance increases until the cable fails like cheap cables will.
The Fusion4K eye test shows a clear area around the "mask" (the middle shape in the eye) in their results. This means that there is no signal loss in the cable and that tells me that the materials used to make the cable are top notch. I found this information with simple internet searches and you can too.
My point is that better cable materials make a better cable and I want the best to future proof my setup. That's why I went with this cable. Also, the cables look great and "feel" well made when I held them next to my old cables. I'm very happy with my purchase.

More then enough power for everything I need to charge or power, and only takes up one plug on the wall. I use this in my lab to power things like Arduino boards and my Raspberry Pi 2, and charge my phone and iPad when they get low without having to take them back downstairs to charge them.
I recently was powering my Rasberry Pi 2 with my 60W, 6 port and accidentally shorted the 5V pin out with the ground pin and the Pi turned off. I couldn't get it to come back on and thought I fried it. If you don't know about the Pi it's a small development computer with open pins for running and controlling other things and it's easy to short something by mistake. I saw that my iPhone and iPad were still charging so I didn't think it was the USB power block. Then I remembered reading something about a short cut off protection built into the IQ system on the these, so I unplugged it from the one USB port and plugged it into another and the computer came back one. So the one port was still off and then I remembered reading about how to reset it. You just unplug it from the wall for 10 seconds and plug back in. So I did just that and all the ports came back to life. That's when I realized that the IQ short protection probably saved my little computer from permanent damage, and also maybe saved my other things plugged in charging also. Most shorts will back feed and could damage other things charging also plugged into the other USB ports. If it didn't have the IQ protection I could have damaged 3 iPhones and a iPad I had charging, and I just got done fixing them also.

I know, in most cases you won't be shorting out anything because you won't be charging or powering something with open pins like a Rasberry Pi, but sometimes electronics them self will fail and short out and could backfeed into the circuit damaging other devices charging. This could save the other things also plugged in and charging if it was to happen.

This was a nice feature to have and probably saved me from having to repair or buy new things. It's not the kind of protection I expect from something that costs as low as this, but I'm glad it had it and has the 18 month warranty. Usable, but not optimal. Using a bench power supply I am able to test this device on input voltages between 0-30 volts. At first everything seemed great, when input voltage was above 6 volts the output was always rock stable at 5v. But that's where the good news stops. After about 4 minutes with no load the TO-92 package device (probably a transistor) next to the input header started getting hot. The higher the input voltage, the hotter it got. The output voltage did stay at 5v. After 10 minutes of sweeping around between 6 volts and 30 volts the TO-92 was way too hot for my liking, and I stopped the testing. I suspect if you stay under 12-14 input voltage you'd be ok, but at this point I'm not risking my downstream USB devices on it.

If your input voltage is below 5volts, it will gladly pass that onto the output voltage (- about 0.7v), which can be bad. Some devices, if they are expecting 5V, and you give them say 3V, they won't be happy, and may damage the downstream device.

[USABILITY]: It's a little hard to actually use. It's got two buttons, Top button is main power, bottom button is output power switch. They are both "soft switches", meaning they are controlled by some form of logic, IE a microprocessor. I suspect the microprocessor is underneath the LED display. In order to get it to start outputting power, first you have to press the top button to turn on the main unit, then it starts displaying input voltage only on the LED, I wasn't able to get it to show anything other then the input voltage. After it's displaying voltage then you press the bottom button and it turns on the output voltage. Not sure why/what they intended that usage for.

Later I'll do a actual destructive test on it and see if it'll fail on me, and if it does fail, what output voltage it'll put out when it does fail.

Pros:

Small Size

Cons:

* Gets way too hot to handle/touch.
* Output voltage can dip below 5V ifinput voltage dips below 6ish volts.
* Have to manipulate buttons to get it to output any voltage.
* LED display only displays incoming voltage, no amperage, no wattage.
* No way to turn off the display, and provide output voltage.
