How the Geek Out 1000 Stacks Up The Geek Out 1000 (or GO1K as it has come to be called by many) is a fabulous little DAC + Headphone Amplifier combo device, but it's not alone.

Since the time of its introduction it has been hailed as one of the best sounding DAC+Amp combos for its size or in its price bracket by numerous hi-fi and audiophile reviewers. It "awesomifies" (a term coined by Gavin Fish, LHLabs' Chief Innovation Officer) virtually every 2-channel digital sound format out there from regular CDs and MP3s to Studio Masters at crazy high resolutions like 32-bit 384kHz. It even plays the exotic-but-beautiful Direct Stream Digital (aka DSD64, aka SACD), a 1-bit 2.8MHz audio format favored by many audiophiles.

I backed the project that gave birth to the Geek Out on Kickstarter years ago coincidentally for $199. Since receiving mine in April of 2014 my Kickstarter Green (or as I like to call it, "Pononite") GO1K has been my "Pride and Joy." I listen to it daily and use a variety of headphones with it. The full watt of Class A power can drive most of the headphones on the planet with aplomb and makes for a nice hand warmer in the winter months as well (this by design -- if you're not familiar with Class A amplifiers, they run hot because unlike the more common Class A/B designs, they never 'switch off' or take a break when the music stops or gets quiet). You can rest assured that the extra warmth isn't a problem: I've run my Geek Out non-stop for months at a time as part of my home audio system with nary a problem.

By way of comparison, I own (or have spent significant time with) several similar combos from other manufacturers, each of which has their relative charms: the Audioquest Dragonfly (1.2), the Meridian Explorer, and the ifi Nano iDSD. The Geek Out stands up proudly in this company. It is more capable than the Dragonfly (both in terms of the range of headphones it can drive and the range of music formats it can play back without prior down-sampling). I also think it sounds better, but it should be noted that the Dragonfly ($149) costs half as much as the GO1K's $299 MSRP, so all of this should come as no surprise. I'm only listing it here because at the time of the Geek Out's introduction, there were very few "truly audiophile" thumb-drive and super-portable options, and the Dragonfly was one of them and worth all of its accolades.

Compared to the similarly priced Meridian Explorer ($349), it is a toss-up at lower playback resolutions. The Explorer excels at 24/96 and below (CD, DVD Audio, etc.). It has a very natural, very musical quality to its presentation that really draws you in. Meridian has a very deep well of experience to draw from here, and it really comes through in the Explorer. The Geek Out also sounds excellent with the same sources, but the presentation is slightly different. I would describe the Geek Out's sound as favoring precision over musicality. The Meridian favors the opposite way, but in most cases, we're talking about subtle shades of difference. It may well be that the electrical characteristics of a given set of headphones and how they relate to each of these amplifiers may well have more tonal impact than anything the DACs are doing. That said, when you step up into the rarefied air of DSD, DXD, and high-res PCM playback, the Geek Out really shines. It may cost less than the Explorer (even at MSRP), but like the Explorer, it "punches far above its pay grade" in terms of quality and capability. At $199, the Geek Out 1000 is a steal!

The similarly priced iFi Nano iDSD DAC ($199) is a great device that actually sports more "native sound format" compatibility than the highly-capable Geek Out in that the Nano can not just "single" rate DSD, but also "double" and "quad" rate DSD (DSD128, DSD256), and all via ASIO without any prior format or source-rate conversion. It also features the sexiest volume control of the bunch, a brilliant silver knob with nearly perfect "feel" to it. It turns smoothly and near the start of its range there is a satisfying spike in resistance followed by a "click" which tells you the device is now On and ready to rock. This kind of sex appeal is only available because of its substantially larger chassis and beautiful industrial design. The Nano *will* fit in your pocket and it can even be affixed to your phone (via provided rubber bands), *and* it even has a built-in rechargeable battery (for jamming with said phone on-the-go or for isolating the DAC from the noisy power that is found in PCs).

All of the little "extras" the Nano has make audiophiles rejoice, but at the end of the day what matters most to us is "how does it sound?" On its own, the Nano sounds great. Like the Geek Out and the rest, it is *vastly* better than the $2 sound chip on your motherboard and even the one in your iPhone or Android... and far more capable; however, when compared side-by-side to the Geek Out (and even the Meridian), its sound comes up a little wanting. The Geek Out 1000 has an "it" quality to its presentation that the Nano lacks. There is a mix of immediacy, musicality, punch, drive, and fullness that embodies the Geek Out's sound which the Nano can't quite manage (at least with my headphones -- I used a pair of Sony's flagship, the MDR Z7, to compare with).

Therefore, I find that the Geek Out is a superior performer to the Nano even though it lacks some of the "creature comforts" of its larger rival. While the volume knob is nice, the delineating factor here truly is the integrated battery -- all things considered, I'd rather spend the same money on a Geek Out 1000 because it sounds better to my ears. In the future, if I decide that I absolutely *must* have a battery, I'd probably take a long listen to the Geek Out V2+ (which has a battery built-in) first. Testimonials from friends and other reviews I've read say that V2 platform sounds even better than the original Geek Out.

There are two drivers for stereo sound, but no specifications are given. Listening to music at lower volumes, the sound is enjoyable. At louder volumes, there is noticeable sibilance and muddiness.

This speaker is designed for outdoor use and is resistant to light splashing in my testing, but no IPX specifications for water resistance are given. The flap over the ports seals tightly.

A USB charging cable and a 3.5 mm audio cable are included, along with a carabiner. The box can be used for storage.

Bose AE2 - Bose Soundtrue Around-Ear

1. The eartips and cord on SoundSports is more durable and it's supposed to resist sweat and some light water. IE2 cords look really fragile, though they have been fine for nearly two years and never had a problem. But I won't use my IE2 running because my sweat will destroy them for sure.

As long as you buy those noise isolating pieces like Westone W4 or Shure SE215, I think the problem will still be there. So do NOT use them in quite libraries or offices. I don't see the problem of having this while working out.

Handy Power Strip if Used Correctly I'm actually quite surprised at the other reviews. I've been using this power strip for awhile and I've never had any issues with it. The setup can be a bit confusing I guess, but you catch on quick after using it. Basically, there are three different settings that you can plug into. There's your standard "always on" outlet, which is exactly as it says. It's always on. It's just like a regular outlet. Then you have the two others, which are coupled. Plugging anything into the master controlled outlets will not get power unless whatever is plugged into the master outlet is on. I always thought this was a great way to save a bit of electricity. I used it by having my TV plugged into the master outlet, and then having external things that I only use for my TV plugged into the master controlled outlets (like my xbox, blue ray player, controller charger, basically anything that the TV needs to be on to use). This product worked just fine for me. If you don't like the setup of the master controlled outlets, however, then I would recommend just buying a standard power strip.

For about 90 bucks, they're great cans.

Head-To-Head with the Turcom HR-903 Speaker [[VIDEOID:36cb8f168cf666f0f37d28296599131a]]When compared head-to-head with the Turcom HR-903, I have to say the Voombox Party does come out the subjectively lesser... but not necessarily in terms of what you are looking for - far smaller sizing being the biggest positive for the Voombox.

Turcom's HR-903 has a stated IP waterproofing rating of 5 (Water jets from all angles) - and I can attest to it's durability as it has been sitting on my pool deck for the past months.

The Voombox doesn't have any IP rating I can find either on the box, the manual, or online - other than \\"Water Resistant\\". Without knowing what kind of internal proofing it has, I would say IPx4 (typical shower speaker level, spray and splashes) based off the grill and the cover flap on the side.

The HR-903 is about 2 and 1/2 times the mass of the Voombox and certainly heavier, and that very well may be a big point for you. Yet, I do frown at the complete lack of any kind of carrying case or such for the Voombox. At this price range, I would expect some sort of case or bag. Or for the HR-903's, an in-built handle.

The controls on the HR-903 are touch sensitive, and can be a problem if water collects inside the little divots. The controls on the Voombox are push buttons under a rugged silicone band - and uses the \\"+\\",\\"-\\" for both Volume and Track (Short Press Volume), whereas it is all separated on the HR-903.

Now for the meat-and-potatoes, audio.

The Voombox certainly holds its own, the 20W volume being pretty much the same level as the 30W put out by the HR-903. Mellow yet clear spectrum with a balance between punchy and rumbly bass response. However, the HR-903 has a more rumbly, more expansive bass response. So it boils down to how much overdriven bass rumble you like. I do like a gritty BEWM. :)

One thing to note about the Voombox, be sure the back or top isn't up against anything - the bass it pushes out will cause rattling buzz within the casing. Also, I found the AUX In to be somewhat disappointing. The volume basically halved, though still sounded great, and will not work with a 4 pole jack (i.e. \\"wired\\" microphone input), just a standard 3 pole.

Won't Connect to the Internet I spent a lot of time researching receivers and thought the Pioneer VSX-1130 would be perfect for my needs.  Unfortunately, I will never know because it would not connect to the internet, which is the first step in setting up the receiver.  The Set Up app on my Android said that the Wi-Fi configuration was complete, but then when I chose the next step of connecting peripherals, the app said that the receiver could not be found.  I verified using the status screen on the receiver that it was not connecting to the internet.  There is nothing wrong with my network.  A Wi-Fi Dish DVR was installed just two weeks ago using the same network and it works like a charm.  If only the Pioneer were designed so well.  Also, I should mention that the Android Navi app crashed a couple of times as well.  It does not get very good reviews overall in the Play store.  Edit 8/27/15:  So I spent many hours trying to get the receiver to connect to the internet.  After setting up the Wi-Fi with no luck, I moved it over to my router and used an Ethernet connection and went through the Pioneer setup app over and over.  No difference.  I went back to the Wi-Fi connection.  After tearing my hair out, I started connecting my A\V components to the receiver without the help of the app.  I was sure I was going to have to ship the receiver back, and then, all of a sudden, it connected.  I did not make any changes to my router settings.  My other internet-connected products have had no problems at all with my network, so I don't know what the problem was with the receiver. However, once connected, I took the opportunity to immediately update to the latest firmware.  The Pioneer has had no trouble keeping the internet connection so far, so I have raised my review rating from one to three stars.  I do want to like this receiver, because it has the specs I want.  My new speakers are still on the way from Amazon, so I will be doing a lot more work with setting up the receiver and will probably have another update to my review.  Edit 9/13/15: Alright, so I got my brand new speakers connected and it sounds great.  I found out that whenever the power supply is interrupted, I have to power cycle my router to get the Pioneer to connect again to the internet.  I don't have this issue with any of my other Wi-Fi devices.  So far, the biggest disappointment is that the Bluetooth music streaming from my less than a year old Motorola phone is marred by constant stuttering.  An old Samsung phone works fine with it.  I should mention that the Motorola Bluetooth has no problems with my other Bluetooth devices.  With all the different brands of phones out there, and different flavors of Android, I probably shouldn't expect everything to work well together.  Edit 10/06/15:  After the annoyances I experienced, I decided to keep the receiver.  I got it on sale for $499.99, and the only other receiver I found with similar features was an Onkyo that was priced $85 higher.  Also, I should mention that the latest firmware upgrade included the addition of HDMI 2.0a support, which means that the Pioneer should now be able to work with the latest HDTV's that have HDR technology.

One of the most valuable yet overlooked features is wiring fault indicators, such as the one found on this APC C25B.
I love protectors with wiring fault indicators because they reveal problems that you may not otherwise know exist. I once had a surge protector wiring fault LED illuminate and subsequently discovered that the outlet was wired incorrectly with the neutral going to the hot side. I’ve had a few other faulty outlets trigger warning LED’s. One was caused by a loose wire and another was caused by a metal housing surrounding the outlet. The speaker is quite large and operates on AC power only (no internal batteries.) It's about 20 1/2\\" wide, 7 3/8\\" tall and 5 3/4\\" deep. Concerning the depth, considering the power cord sticking ouf of the back, it's actually going to require a minimum of 7 1/4\\" of depth to accommodate the plug. And you'll want to leave a bit of room to maximize the sound due to the bass ports being on the back of the speaker.

The power supply/adapter has two cords... an AC power cord that is 6' in length which goes from the wall into the power supply and then a thinner 6' cord that connects the power supply to the speaker.

The enclosure is made of wood (actually MDF a manufactured wood product), not plastic and that is one of the reasons this speaker has superior sound. On the top of the speaker are a number of touch controls. From left to right you have a brightness button (High, Low, Off) then the power button that also switches between Bass and Treble mode with -5 to +5 adjustment range. Next is the Volume - and Volume + buttons.

On the back is a bluetooth pairing reset button, as well as a 3.5mm Aux In port, master power switch and a USB, 2.1A output port to charge and power any USB devices such as the tablet or smartphone providing the music.

The speaker comes with two sets of feet. You can choose to use rubber domed feet or steel spiked feet. Your speaker placement and/or your preference would determine which set of feet you end up using. The rubber feet stick on via double sided tape while the metal feet screw into the bottom of the speaker.

The speaker is very powerful and will easily fill a large room with big sound. This is a great party speaker but also is excellent for normal listening levels as the clarity of sound is fantastic. Bass is big in this speaker and the fact that you can customize the bass and treble to your liking is a real plus.

You do not get a remote with the speaker, nor is a remote available. You cannot change tracks from the speaker and it does not include a hands free function for your smartphone. You use your device to change tracks and of course your device also allows you to adjust music level as well as use any sound equalization presets that your device may provide in addition to the bass and treble controls on the speaker.

This sound great with all types of music. Bass lovers will be very happy with the bass that this speaker is capable of providing. The dual 5\\" woofers can really put out some great low end. But this is not a bass heavy speaker... the highs are crisp and balanced nicely with the mids.

I initially thought that the AC power was being stopped because the input from the transformer might have come loose, so I arranged to it to be attached more securely, but the same thing still happened, even though there was no one near the connection when the interruption occurred. I then went to battery power, but the projection system does not work on battery power, so I used both the battery and AC in hopes that if there was an interruption in the AC then the battery backup would prevent the clock from resetting, but it does not. Even a broken clock is right twice a day, but when this clock resets it is never right, and gives an erroneous time. I have therefore had to downgrade from two to only one star.

Original review
I do not recommend this clock for the reasons described below. The clock worked and I purchased it on a half price closeout, so as a clock it was OK, but overpriced if you just operate it as a simple digital clock, hence two stars instead of the minimum one.

Why do I call this a “brain dead” - described below in order of the most annoying features first:
· The projector feature is poorly designed. When you face the clock, it projects the time on the wall behind or above the clock upside down and backwards. The time is projected correctly on the wall facing the clock and can therefore be read when you are facing this wall and have your back towards the clock. However, this most likely requires projecting the time more than the six foot focusing distance, as it did in my case. The result is a large somewhat blurry image. The correct orientation is also displayed when you turn the clock with its back facing you, so you can only read the projected time on the wall facing the clock. BETTER PROJECTOR CLOCKS HAVE THE ABILITY TO FLIP THE IMAGE IN ORDER TO CORRECT FOR THIS, and give you the ability to view the correct image with the clock in a different orientation relative to the way that you are facing. Also, while the projector can be rotated about one axis, that is all. Therefore, I found it impossible to orient both the clock and the projected image to optimum orientations.

· The clock face is tilted backwards at a fixed angle, which cannot be adjusted. This made it difficult to read the clock while lying in bed, and required me to make a jury-rigged system to keep the face at an orientation where I could read the clock. Unfortunately, the clock was less stable in this position, requiring still further modifications. Even a moderately thoughtful deign would have eliminated this problem without adding to the coat of the clock.

· The temperature readings were three degrees high (compared to two other digital thermometers in the room). This may seem petty, but if you are interested on knowing the temperature and its changes over a period of days you should at least see the correct value. This incorrect value may be due to the heat given off by the projecting LED and there is no way to turn off the projector, except to run completely on batteries. (The clock can be run completely on battery power, or with the batteries as a backup for a power failure but unused when the clock is running on AC.)

· The clock is very bright, perhaps too bright when you are trying to sleep and there is no way to reduce the brightness. The numbers are 1/2 an inch high as opposed to ¾ of an inch on other clocks. Instead of a larger image this clock has color bands that go up and down and cycle, illustrating the temperature changes over the last five days. The bands take up most of the lower half of the clock face and I found them to be distracting, so I had to cover over this feature, as there is no way to turn it off.

· Setting the clock up was a pain – not at all intuitive and probably almost impossible without the instructions, so if you lose them the clock might become useless.

All in all this is a prime example of a poor (brain dead) design. The clock would have been more useful as more than a simple clock if the clock face could be tilted and more useful as a projector clock if the projected image could be rotated about more than one axis and flipped so that it could be read when one was facing the clock, instead of only when the clock face is not also visible. This is a great little device for ~$20, as long as you keep in mind that it's ~$20 OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

Changed my life on airplanes This review will concentrate on using these on airplanes. I have seen folks for years with headsets on airplanes, but I have always just used either the ones supplied by the flight, or sometimes my own earbud style. The earbuds however are just too uncomfortable to wear for long periods. Recently, I had to travel to Australia from the US, and that involves some very long flights. Upon arrival in Sydney, my ears hurt and I was pretty tired from lack of sleep. While waiting for a connection, I saw some TKD brand noise canceling headphones on sale for $99 in the airport. I also tried on the Bose QC25, but I just couldn't bring myself to spend $300, so I took a chance and bought the TDK NC 400.

The TDK NC400 were OK. The ear muffs were round, so I guess they are knows as "on the ear" style, not "over the ear". The noise canceling worked, but I wasn't overwhelmed by it, and in part that is probably due to the ear muff not really covering my ears, so a little sound gets past the muffs. They also weren't super comfortable. Again, this is the ear muff style, not a brand thing. After a few hours more flying, I realized that a really good noise canceling headset could make a difference. Three weeks later, heading back through Sydney, I purchased these Bose QC25 and wore them all the way back to JFK; about 20 hours of flying. I will never fly without them again.

They were the most comfortable way to listen to music or watch the in-flight movies I have ever worn. The noise canceling is outstanding, and I really didn't hear the background noise at all. At one point, I turned off the music and just left the noise canceling on, and I slept for about 6 hours without disturbance. I felt much more rested when we arrived in LA than I ever had after 15 hours of flying.

When they are on my head, I can barely even feel them as they are so light and the cushioning is so soft and well made. They are very easy to adjust and don't pinch on your head.

I can only compare these to the TDK NC400 that I also had. In my opinion, there is no comparison - the Bose are in a completely different league. Yes, they are 3 times the price, but I have to admit that they are 3 times better.

PROS:
- super comfortable
- amazing noise canceling
- really nice carry case.

CONS:
- not wireless (would be a nice feature)
- not even discrete.
- large muffs may interfere with your ability to rest your head on a pillow when compared to earbuds

If you are thinking about noise canceling headsets, I would urge you to consider these. Using them for a 15 hour flight made me a believer.

RCA vs. Sennheiser I just bought my second set of these. I'm shocked they are still selling this model as i got my first set back in the early 2000's when they were 80 dollars in stores. they lasted me 9 years of uber brutal heavy, "dear god how could you do that to them" use. yeah i broke them. i broke them alot.. super glue to the rescue every time. let me explain the extent of my abuse. I work at home with my hands, i do all chores in this household too. I get bored of music all the time, so instead i get my computer to read me novels, audio book, or by text to speech. i am not picky. over those 9 years i probably have funneled about 2000 novels thru these babies. Day in, day out use... i've probably fallen asleep wearing them 500 or 600 times... other times i took them off and left them on my bed next to me while i slept.. and then they would fall 2.5 feet to the concrete floor, and i may or may not step on them in the morning while rolling out of bed.. there is no such thing as a pair of headphones i can't break. thankfully i am also good at fixing things too... the old ones have been broken in about 5 different places. first thing to brake was the swivel to get the angle right on your head.. lots of super glue fixed that. a tip though is to figure out the correct angle for your head so you can have them turned back at a comfortable angle. then the second angle on the other side broke. then the bar that holds onto the ribbon thingy that holds the head strap in place broke it's mount.. but if you took the screws out there are internal bits inside the grey part that you can just loop the ribbon onto and screw closed.. i think i had to fix the other side a year later.. then i broke one of the parts that holds onto the ear muff... honestly i can't remember what i did to fix that.. i probably splinted a wire on it to make a new pivot though. i'm sure, with normal use and people won't have to deal with as many breakages as i did. because wearing headphones for 16 hours a day for 9 years straight i am sure is not normal use. their final death 9 years later happened while on vacation... i don't think the antenna base likes being packed away into a suitcase and driven 400 miles yearly.. on the 9th year the base died.. on inspection because i opened it.. the circuit board was cracked in half... which i soldered back together and got 3 or 4 months more out of it before well.. i dunno.. i am not the greatest solderer... R.I.P. RCA WHP141.. Hello Sennheiser TR 140. the rest of the review will be a comparison between the rca vs. sennheiser.
lets talk performance. Snap Crackle POP! rca has no features to protect your ears from the crackling noises that happen when you are way too far away from the base. sennheiser does... sennheiser will mute your feed to save you from a loud pop and replace it with a very annoying beeping noise... grrrrr i hate you beeping... but you get uset to it after a few months.. i don't even get annoyed anymore truthfully.
So yeah, that last
statement makes you go oh hell yeah i like no painful crackles right? well it's at a cost.. which brings us to our next topic.. range.... honestly.. rca says 150, back then sennheiser said 350.. i was super excited about the extra range as my 70' by 25' ranch style house didn't get full coverage as the 150 foot range does not include walls.. so, 3 of my walls = 25 foot range with some interference on rca, and sennheiser, the liars... well, the antenna strength is identical... there was absolutely no difference in signal strength.. range would be identical if it wasn't for the snap crackle pop interference feature.. so, if you go 3 walls away, and you held your head juuuuuust right, you could hold an ok signal for maybe 20 seconds before it cuts out and beeps at you.. so listening without beeps is more like 2 walls away instead of 3 walls with rca... so yeah... range is better on the rca then those super expensive sennheisers...
but wait... that sounds too good tobe true right? cheaper rca being better then sennheiser? yeah.. it is.. this brings us to ergonomics... this is where sennheiser blows rca out of the water and reigns supreme.. i can't say enough good things about sennheiser's ergonomics.. the comfort levels of just wearing the 2 different headphones... rca are like wearing 4 inch high heels, vs, sennheiser feeling like super comfy sneakers that are perfectly molded to your feet just for you.. now.. lets get this straight.. if your wearing rca for 4 hours of tv use... no problem.. 16 hours and then falling asleep wearing them multiple times a week... let me explain what doing that will do to you... before i ever wore wireless headphones my ears stuck out... if they stuck out any bit more then they did, i know i would of been ruthlessly teased for them.. having constant pressure on your ears to be folded back for years on end.. yeah.. my ears are the perfect distance required by beauty now.. about a 10 degree angle difference... beauty is painful.. including unintentional beauty.. i wore the rca headphones too much... they occasionally gave me bed sores in the cartilage of my ears and i'd have to take a week off of wearing them for my ears to heal. I've been using my sennheisers for... oh... 5 or 6 years now? not totally sure.. but i've never once had sore ears from them..
audio performance.. i'm not an audiophile rca sounds like any old wired pair of headphones i've ever used... it works and works less good the further from the base. if your very far it is reminiscent of walkie talkies.. sennheiser audio performance? thats a hard one.. the sound is very very different from rca.. i remember when i first switched over i absolutely HATED it.. it sounds muffled and super clear at the same time.. really hard to explain.. i'm years into using them so.. i no longer care what it sounds like anymore... besides, i am trying to listen to an audio book, or a computer generated voice... i just want to understand words... both work for that perfectly..
Why am i switching back to rca whp141 from sennheiser the top of the line wireless headphones world wide you ask? well.. i am not totally switching back.. see.. my sennheisers have a problem.. one which involves me soldering.. and we know how well that worked out... and the problem with the sennheisers are my own fault... extremely my fault.. so, by the time i got my sennheisers i figured out how to abuse headphones for as long as i wanted to.. 24 hours if i wanted.. just have a second set of batteries charging at the same time.. switch out the batteries.. see, on both rca and sennheiser... they do a trickle charge to recharge my rechargeable batteries... and that's just not fast enough.. they do that because it extends the life of the batteries.. and under normal use this is great... but no, i gotta wear them 16+ hours. so i would be changing the batteries at least daily and sometimes twice a day when the batteries where towards the end of their life... sennheiser doesn't make the ear covers or the battery bay strong enough to have that many battery changes.... we are talking in the hundreds... (i repaired my ear covers from falling off with magnets) so, when i lean forward the batteries no longer are in contact with the contacts.. and they turn off.. i lean back and they are fine.. this is driving me batty... because when i do chores or make jewelry i lean forward... soooooooo.. eventually i will mount an outer battery case and solder the leads onto the battery posts on my sennheiser.. but.. well.. i'm not the greatest solderer.. so i keep on putting it off.... and..... i want my range back so i can work in my garden again.. sooo... rca whp141, welcome back... rca, i won't be using to as my mains... you hurt my ears too much, but when i want the range.. you will be there for me.. and sennheiser will be there for me long before my ears begin to hurt.. best of both worlds! yay!..
as for my advice of which to get. if your a normal user and won't wear them a ridiculous amount of time like me.. get rca whp141 and save that extra 100-ish bucks for something else, if your ridiculous like me listening to now somewhere over 3400 books... you might want to go with sennheiser.. your ears will thank you.
p.s. durability on sennheiser is alot better then rca.. if i wasn't doing any battery changes then i suspect i would have almost no damage to my sennheisers (excluding the missing head pad, and weird warping shape falling asleep in them has created (pad got loose because i kept on trying to straighten the warping) soo, both issues.. my fault)

Very nice *for the price*, much better than similar ones OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

packed with practical features and good sound too. I receive many many bluetooth speakers to review so I have gotten fairly well acquainted with the nuanced differences between them. The speaker manufacturers are always looking for a way to set their speaker apart because with the ubiquity of these speakers they need to find a niche that would have buyers spending on their product over they're competition's product.

Enter the BV350.... This is a true rugged outdoor speaker. The company has supplied it with a bicycle mount (similar to the water bottle mount) so that you can easily affix it to your bike or pull it off of your bike and tote it with you. It comes with a karabiner for attaching to your belt loop or backback as you partake in outdoor activity.

ONE OF THE BEST FEATURES OF THIS SPEAKER.... is the easy to manipulate dedicated physical volume dial located at the top of the unit. If bluetooth speakers have volume buttons, all too often those buttons are shared with the "previous song/next song" button. If you are riding your bike at a good clip and you want to turn up the volume, you don't want to be fumbling with a shared button.... half the time when I hit those shared buttons to turn up the volume because I like a particular song, I hit it the wrong way and end up skipping to the next song. Trust me, this volume dial is a real pleasure.

But a volume dial alone isn't' enough to make a speaker into a five star wonder. Sound is probably the most critical, no? The sound on this is very good. Not the best I've heard in the portable speaker lineup but definitely very respectable. The sound favors the mid ranges and high notes but it is not tinny and there is some discernible bass. If you are a bass junkie this probably wont satisfy you but for the rest of us it gives enough hint of bass to make it pleasurable to listen to. I tried assorted music genres and all sounded good.

This speaker is a bit larger than the uber portable ones you might bring along on a hike but for going from bicycle to indoors to a day at the beach, I think this is the speaker you will want. The fact that it is waterproof (go ahead, shower with it. You'll be amazed) makes it great for all sorts of situations where you might want music. And along bluetoothing to your phone, there is a tf slot (you might know it as a micro sd slot) for playing music directly from a card. So, while the sound isn't absolutely the best sound I've heard out of these budget portables, it is still pretty terrific and the added features (waterproof, dedicated easy to use volume dial, bike mountable, sd card slot) make this without a doubt a five star speaker. I have absolutely no hesitation recommending it. As the young man I gave it to exclaimed when he got it... "this is sick" And all his friends agreed. Sick indeed.

BOTTOM LINE: This is a feature rich and very practical portable and waterproof bluetooth speaker. Bass is there but not terribly pronounced. Overall solid sound.

Sound Multiplication Equals Whole New Level of Bluetooth Sound [[VIDEOID:650269cb170c560d01c58b48656739f3]]What's better than a single Bluetooth speaker? Two! And even better than that? Throw in one of those new Bluetooth transmitters than can pair TWO Bluetooth speakers at once, and get... FOUR!

Paired with Samsung Galaxy S6; paired with a DBPower Bluetooth Transmitter/Receiver in conjunction with Artchros Bluetooth Dual (Wired) Speakers and AUX sourced from my S6. Also later added in the Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 as a third \\"Buddy\\".

Audio Characteristics:
As a single speaker, rich, full spectrum with bumping bass, especially when you put on that little casing on the bottom - yet just not that loud. Good, comfortable volume when right-near-by... it does open up quite a bit, though, when you put two together.

The AUX Out, e.g. the \\"Buddy Stereo\\" seems to work best with I assume shadow powered speakers, like another UB+ that is turned off, so I am guessing the main unit (whichever one is turned on and actively paired) supplies power to the \\"Buddy\\". The AUX Out cord goes from Buddy Stereo to Buddy Stereo port, and not in the other AUX In port on the speaker, which also leads me to believe there is some special wiring going on inside.

**Update: These use four pole AUX cables (e.g. three rings around the jack) - will NOT work with typical three pole jacks (two rings around the jack). This may explain why the crackling I got on the Roar 2. Something to take note of if you are wanting to use a much longer cable (and there isn't much on Amazon in four pole, long audio cables, but I did buy a ten footer male to female extension from KableDirect).**

Still I did try out the Y-splitter that comes with each UB+ Eupho on a Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2, and it resulted in some crackly, crackly power interference until I gently fiddled with the cord. And yes, it seems older reviews took the Y-splitter as merely a way to connect two sources into one speaker. I immediately saw it the other way around. Three UB+ Euphos! But that also probably leads to a much shorter battery life (if I am right about the shadow powering).

**Update: I did get direct confirmation about daisy chaining UB+ Euphos - you can chain as many as you like with the splitter (apparently the biggest test was with FIFTY of them at once). No word about actual battery impact, but I can say its really good even with two.**

BATTERY LONGEVITY & COMPARATIVE MARKET PRICING:
20 Hours is when you have a single speaker playing at a moderate level; that is an outstanding battery for a speaker this size. On average, the play time is more like 4-5 hours for similar sized speakers in the budge range. Once you get around $25 +, the play time tends to improve to 8 to 10 hours. Here, twenty hours! The only other Bluetooth speaker I have that matched the play time is an Anker speaker I bought last year, specifically because of the incredible play time, and also priced at around $40. So that is the comparative market range this speaker, as a single, truly belongs in. However, if you have shopped about like I have for dual wired speakers that are Bluetooth enabled, 80 bucks for a set that has great audio response AND tiny footprint is also quite favorably comparative. That Artchros set I have cost me $50, and it does have far less bass sustainability than these put together.

As another example, iDeaUSA is selling a pair of dual synched Bluetooth speakers (no intervening wire) for $80 - yet those require a particularly strong, stable Bluetooth connection (like a Personal Computer) and didn't work with my DBPower transmitter... and are the much larger standard-sized speakers.

The UB+ Eupho does actively play while being concurrently powered by a USB source - just be aware that for most 5V rechargeable battery powered devices, this can have a negative impact on the battery capacity.

SUMMARY:
Gong back to the similarly priced, similarly rich sounding, similarly long life Anker Bluetooth speaker, the UB+ is a huge step forward with the \\"Buddy\\" connection. If Anker had the foresight last year to allow the same capability, I would have long purchased a second. Now, I am pondering purchasing a third one to try connecting via the Y-splitter. Would love to run one more behind me.... mmmm, Android gaming immersion. >Insert Homer Simpson Drooling Here<

I have a 55” Samsung TV whose speakers, like most, are in the back. I had it set up with a couple floor speakers but the amp died, and I replaced the setup with this. The Bose website says it can be used as a base for most 46"-50" TVs.

First, this is NOT a sound bar. It measures 14” from front to back, 24.75” wide, and 3” high. Anyway, there are three 2-inch speakers in the front middle, and one on each side toward the front so sound is distributed quite well throughout the room. There is no separate subwoofer, but I don’t find one necessary.

The thing can really get loud. You can adjust the amount of base you prefer, and there is a dialog mode if you want voices emphasized and the background diminished. This works well. The quality of the sound when streaming music over bluetooth is awesome, like high-class speakers with well-rounded sound from treble to bass. No tininess to be found. The sound when listening to TV is really impressive--you can actually hear all those subtle things that the closed captions tell you are happening but you couldn’t hear before. The back of the unit has inputs for analog (one red, one white RCA ports), optical, and coaxial cables. It comes with an optical cable, RCA cables, and a power cord. I connected the supplied universal remote to my TV, Apple TV, and DVD player in the space of about 30 minutes. Perfect? Of course not. But a nice device for the price. OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

Great for both music and movies: Energy RC70 + LCR + RCR + RC10 I have been an audiophile for about 4 decades. Over the years, I have used the finer speakers made by AR, JBL, Ohm...eventually settled on Carver ALS-3+ more than 15 years ago and have been very happy with it, no thought of ever replacing them. Since the early days of surround sound, I have also had a home theater system as well. The speakers in that system included Advent, Boston Acoustic, Jamo, Mirage, Polk Audio and Yamaha. I never paid attention to Energy speakers because it's not a highly recognized name in the US and I have never had a chance to see or hear them in the showrooms of hi-fi stores before they pretty much became extinct. About 5 years ago, I came across the RC50 on clearance sale for a modest sum, thought I would take a chance to order a pair. It was immediately obvious that it was better than any of the front speakers I ever had in my HT system. That prompted me to get 5 more RC speakers to revamp all my HT speakers except for the subwoofer: 2 RC-R for the rear, LCR for front center, and RC10 for front surround. They were all on some kind of clearance discount, probably because the company was sold to Klipsch and had some new models coming out. I later came across the Veritas V5.2c center that was supposed to be the reincarnation of the LCR. I bought one to see how it compared. The Veritas' wood finish was superb, but the old LCR is the clear winner in sound quality. After playing the Veritas long enough to be sure that it's not an issue with break-in, I returned it for a refund, something that I rarely do. I was aware that RC70 was the flagship model in the product line, but it was unavailable at the time. Some months later, an authorized dealer's web site showed that there would be a forthcoming stock. I pre-ordered a pair with no hesitation, got them a few months later to replace the RC50. That completed the upgrade.

What distinguishes the RC speakers is the lack of coloration and distortion, i.e., the tonal balance is very neutral, voices and instruments sound smooth, natural and clear. The sound quality is consistent across the product line, matched much better than other company's. The tiny RC10 sounds very much like the big RC70, except a little shy in the bass, but there is enough that many marveled at how big its bass sounded. Putting on the grilles softens the treble a bit. They're magnetically attached, could be easily removed or reattached as one feels like, no worry about breaking some mechanical clips. The appearance also changes with the grille off. The silver/black drivers set in real wood veneer gives an aggressive "robocop" kind of look. This is very practical if a driver ever needs to be replaced. All that's need is to take out a few screws and the driver can be pulled off from the front. I actually had to do that once. Energy sent me a 6.5" driver and it took just a few minutes to make the swap. Were it not covered by the 5-yr warranty, the cost would have been about $60, minimal sum in hi-fi repair. So as long as the company lives, one doesn't need to worry about the RC speaker ever dying. I don't think I'll ever have to think about "upgrading" this 7 speaker HT system.

The tonal quality of the RC70 is actually not that different from the Carver. Both are smooth and neutral. I've found myself using the RC system more and more for listening to music as there are growing numbers of concert DVDs and multichannel music recordings available (SACD, BluRay Audio, DVD Audio, etc.) For most music, the RC70 has a bass that's good enough. The spec goes down to 31 Hz, but that's at -10db level. It could benefit from a subwoofer. I use a Mirage BPS-150i, which is my first and last sub. It works with the RC70 nicely both for music and movies. It doesn't cause an earthquake in the house, but more than my spouse can stand.

Many owners of RC speakers commented that they're incredible value. They seem to have a small random supply that would suddenly appear and then quickly sold out. In recent years, they're offered at a fraction of their original MSRP, and so nothing else could approach that quality/price ratio. Klipsch bought the company but didn't really market the orphaned products to meet the demand. RC70, RC-10 and RC-LCR are still shown on the company web site as current products. I think they actually taken off for a few years and brought back from the grave. This is very rare except for special products that have a real following. Works well, no issues. Modern electronics. This compact USB device works well for receiving GPS. The main 'brain' of this unit is a chipset called U-blox7 which is a modern GPS device designed by (and made for) UBlox, a Swiss fabless semi-conductor company which specializes in high quality communications and positioning components.

This receiver receives the USA medium-earth orbiting GPS satellites as well as the Russian GLONASS positioning satellites system plus several other supplementary satellites that are in certain parts of the world to supplement reception.

When the device is 'locked' onto several satellites, the yellow LED flashes once a second to show that it has a constant lock on the GPS satellites.

Full technical specifications are available in a comprehensive document from u-blox.com which detail full features of the device and cover commands that it accepts if you wish to program the devices many options youself. (document "u-Blox7 Receiver Description including Protocol Specification" - a 209 page document in English for geeks).

The receiver is compatible with the Industry Standard NMEA (National Marine Electronics Association) command language which ensures that it is compatible with a wide variety of standard software.

Drivers are available also from Ublox which work well with this device. I installed for Windows 7 Professional Edition without issues. It also works on Windows XP, Windows 8, Linux. I do not know if it is compatible with Windows 10 yet.

Good headphones for the price These are some nice headphones. They offer good sound quality for a good price. I have worn them for a few hours at a time and they are quite comfortable. There does seem to be a noise cancellation feature that activates itself out of your control. This feature seems to help a bit, but it's not in the same league as my Bose QuietComfort 25 headphones.

The cable is detachable so that you don't need to buy a whole new pair of headphones if the cable gets mangled, which is a nice feature I usually see only in more premium models. The cord, at about four feet long, is a bit shorter than I would like for use with a desktop computer. It leaves little room for motion there. However it's an ideal length for connecting to a laptop or cell phone, with not enough slack to trip over when walking. The sound input on the headphones is just a standard 1/8" headphone jack, so a longer cable could easily be substituted for those who want one and are willing to go without the inline mic and control button.

These headphones are designed in an almost symmetrical fashion. It's not immediately obvious which side should be worn on the left and which side should be worn on the right. After some inspection I was able to discover "L" and "R" markings on the inside of the headband. It's really easy to put these on backwards. They start to feel just a little bit funny after a while when you do that. I'm sure I'll get used to the cord being on the left side.

Overall, these headphones are a great choice for those who don't want to spend a lot of money. Though more expensive headphones can definitely offer a better experience, these get you most of the way there and for a fraction of the cost.

Pono Player intentionally designed to make CD audio sound worse? It has been demonstrated that hi res audio files, like the one PonoMusic store sells, may or may not offer sonic differences over CD audio. When they do, it's because it's a different master of the CD.

However, the PonoPlayer is designed to make your CD audio sound worse than a higher sampled version of the same exact song (not a re-master). Stereophile measured the PonoPlayer's output and found that when using 44.1 sampling rate (that of standard CD audio quality), the treble is slightly rolled off within the range of human hearing from what it should be. In other words, if you take the same CD audio file and resample it to a higher sampling rate--like the hi res audio on PonoMusic--it will sound better with the high res file because the original is not being played accurately, but with slightly less highs, which tends to affect how one perceives detail in music.

So definitely not a good player for CD audio. Get yourself a FiiO X3 or X5 for that. And then if you buy a hi res song from Pono Music and compare it to your CD quality version, how will you ever know if its actually better?

Is this design flaw intentional? Impossible to know. But it certainly does deceptively work to encourage people to buy Pono Music.

5 stars at the low $20 price, but be aware of some limitations (detailed below) OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

Brain Dead Design, Which Malfunctions – 1* Update – I have had to stop using this clock after several months of operation. The clock just stops momentarily, resetting to 12:00 midnight on Jan 1. I initially thought that the AC power was being stopped because the input from the transformer might have come loose, so I arranged to it to be attached more securely, but the same thing still happened, even though there was no one near the connection when the interruption occurred. I then went to battery power, but the projection system does not work on battery power, so I used both the battery and AC in hopes that if there was an interruption in the AC then the battery backup would prevent the clock from resetting, but it does not. Even a broken clock is right twice a day, but when this clock resets it is never right, and gives an erroneous time. I have therefore had to downgrade from two to only one star.

Original review -
I do not recommend this clock for the reasons described below. The clock worked and I purchased it on a half price closeout, so as a clock it was OK, but overpriced if you just operate it as a simple digital clock, hence two stars instead of the minimum one. Note that this clock is sold by numerous vendors at varying prices. While not noted here, this is model 2200.

Why do I call this a “brain dead” - described below in order of the most annoying features first:
· The projector feature is poorly designed. When you face the clock, it projects the time on the wall behind or above the clock upside down and backwards. The time is projected correctly on the wall facing the clock and can therefore be read when you are facing this wall and have your back towards the clock. However, this most likely requires projecting the time more than the six foot focusing distance, as it did in my case. The result is a large somewhat blurry image. The correct orientation is also displayed when you turn the clock with its back facing you, so you can only read the projected time on the wall facing the clock. BETTER PROJECTOR CLOCKS HAVE THE ABILITY TO FLIP THE IMAGE IN ORDER TO CORRECT FOR THIS, and give you the ability to view the correct image with the clock in a different orientation relative to the way that you are facing. Also, while the projector can be rotated about one axis, that is all. Therefore, I found it impossible to orient both the clock and the projected image to optimum orientations.

· The clock face is tilted backwards at a fixed angle, which cannot be adjusted. This made it difficult to read the clock while lying in bed, and required me to make a jury-rigged system to keep the face at an orientation where I could read the clock. Unfortunately, the clock was less stable in this position, requiring still further modifications. Even a moderately thoughtful deign would have eliminated this problem without adding to the cost of the clock.

· The temperature readings were three degrees high (compared to two other digital thermometers in the room). This may seem petty, but if you are interested on knowing the temperature and its changes over a period of days you should at least see the correct value. This incorrect value may be due to the heat given off by the projecting LED and there is no way to turn off the projector, except to run completely on batteries. (The clock can be run completely on battery power, or with the batteries as a backup for a power failure but unused when the clock is running on AC.)

· The clock is very bright, perhaps too bright when you are trying to sleep and there is no way to reduce the brightness. The numbers are 1/2 an inch high as opposed to ¾ of an inch on other clocks. Instead of a larger image this clock has color bands that go up and down and cycle, illustrating the temperature changes over the last five days. The bands take up most of the lower half of the clock face and I found them to be distracting, so I had to cover over this feature, as there is no way to turn it off.

· Setting the clock up was a pain – not at all intuitive and probably almost impossible without the instructions, so if you lose them the clock might become useless.

All in all this is a prime example of a poor (brain dead) design. The clock would have been more useful as more than a simple clock if the clock face could be tilted and more useful as a projector clock if the projected image could be rotated about more than one axis and flipped so that it could be read when one was facing the clock, instead of only when the clock face is not also visible. Usability: 4 Stars
You turn it on by holding the power down, you pair by holding the play button down until you hear the pairing sound. There are no icons to indicate that this is the procedure for pairing. You have to already know, look it up, or guess (and since many other bluetooth speakers pair through the button button or a dedicated pairing button it's not certain you will). Once you get this down it works like any other bluetooth device and it remembers the last 8 paired devices. One nice thing is that it does come with an Audio-in jack with an Aux cable, which is a nice fallback that will keep it usable even if technology changes.

Power Bank: 3 Stars
The power bank aspect is very limited. It's great for keeping the speaker portable and cordless, but as a charger it has the following flaws: 1) It only charges if the speaker is on, even if it's plugged in. This means if you don't want to use it as a speaker, you can't charge. 2) The unit automatically powers down after 90 minutes of Bluetooth inactivity, so charging will end too. 3) The unit is heavy, so you aren't likely going to carry this out into the remote wilderness or anytime you're walking with it. So chances are you'll have other, less complicated power sources for your phone. 4) Once it runs out of battery, you have to use it's proprietary charging plug, so if you left it behind and used up the battery to charge your tablet... then you're out of business until you get home. On the plus side, if you travel internationally, they provide adapters for nearly everywhere in the world.

Decent but quality control could improve. Sewell seems to be savvy at filling a niche market with cabling products for discerning "cine-mediaphiles" and audiophiles. The wires sound good however, you'll want to do an inspection of connection points, like the jacket and composite connector to ensure they are not separating, exposing the shielding underneath.

Try a gentle test bend at each end. In this case, the wire remains functional and electrically sound however the jacket separated from the connector plug. The 12 gauge speaker wires are sound transparent, claiming high strand counts and upscale connectors. Unfortunately troubleshooting intermittent signaling to one channel was required leading to a discovery that the set screws located under the milled barrel covers, which hold the actual wire in place were all loose to varying degrees. The barrels themselves were also an issue because of loose thread tolerances. Loctite resolved this issue. Tightening these screws resolved the continuity issue and now the sound output is great.

Good - the performance claims seem valid
Bad - Quality Control is spotty requiring inspection to avoid electrical issues.

Troubleshoot the product to resolve issues. Or, find some other cabling product.
